speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in addressing the house yesterday with respect to the speech from the throne, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) divided his remarks under three main heads. He referred first to matters of domestic concern, next, to those matters which have to do with imperial affairs, and finally to questions that have an international bearing. I was endeavouring to follow him in the order in which he had proceeded and had to a considerable extent concluded what I had to say with reference to the first division, which, by the way, constituted the longest portion of his utterances.
With respect to matters that are more or less ef domestic concern, there were a few

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
points to which my -hon. friend referred and to which I had not had time to reply when six o'clock came. As to these I shall endeavour in as few words as possible to give him the information which I think he wished to have, and also to address to him a question or two in reference to the significance of his own remarks.
My hon. friend mentioned that we on this side of the house had laid a good deal of stress on the importance of taking parliament as much as possible into our confidence, and wherever it could be so arranged, giving to parliament in the first instance information on matters of national concern, and certainly not making binding commitments without first obtaining the assent of this chamber and where advisable of parliament as a whole. I entirely agree with my hon. friend that such is the desirable course to pursue, and I assure him that such is the wish of the administration; and not only is it the wish, but it has been, and will continue to be, the practice, of the administration in so far as it can possibly be maintained. But I am sure my hon. friend will realize that during the parliamentary recess, when many months elapse between one session and another, situations will arise in which the government is certain to find it necessary to act immediately, and to come to parliament later on with a reasonable explanation of why the matter in question had not been held over for final decision until the members were assembled.
One of the matters to which my hon. friend referred was the announcement by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) that it had been decided that Fort Churchill should be the ocean terminus of the Hudson Bay railway, and I think my hon. friend made the statement that the Minister of Railways and Canals had not only failed to take parliament into his confidence in making that announcement, but had failed even to take his own colleagues into his confidence. I should like to set my hon. friend's mind at rest at once in regard to the latter statement.
I recall the circumstances very well. Mr. Palmer was engaged first of all to make the study which he did with regard to the Hudson Bay bemuse of his acknowledged reputation as an estuarial engineer of pre-eminence, of greater pre-eminence, I assume, than any other engineer engaged in like pursuits, and when he was retained it was assumed that the government was asking for his expert advice not for academic purposes, merely, but rather to be guided in its decision by the best advice that was obtainable. When Mr. PalmeT
made his investigation it was with a view' to giving the government the benefit of his expert opinion, to enable it to decide in the interests of the country which was the most desirable port at which to have the ocean terminus of the Hudson Bay railway. While Mr. Palmer was making his investigation, the question naturally came up as to whether the announcement of the decision which would be made by him should be deferred until parliament assembled, or whether an immediate announcement should be made. The situation was canvassed to some extent between members of the government and the Minister of Railways and Canals before the minister went to the west with Mr. Palmer. It was felt that if Mr. Palmer was in a position to give his decision immediately, there was every reason why that opinion should be made known also to the country with as little delay as possible. Let me just ask my hon. friend what his -criticism would have been if, having Mr. Palmer's opinion, we had withheld it. If, having had in our possession the opinion of an expert engineer who was to determine which was the better port, we had held back any announcement of his decision for several months, we would have been justly criticized on the ground that it was for reasons which affected the interests of friends of the government or something of the kind, and I think we would have been entitled to that criticism if we had taken that attitude. It was precisely because we wished to avoid any possible criticism, and also because we believed that in other respects it was in the national interest to give the country the information at the earliest opportunity, that it was decided before his report was made that the government should -take prompt action with respect to announcing the decision of its expert.
May I -add this? Far from failing to take his colleagues into his confidence in the matter, I recall very distinctly receiving from my colleague the Minister of Railways and Canals a telegram at the time the report had been finally made saying that the report was now in readiness and asking if I would ascertain from other members of the government their views in the matter, and give him the decision of council with respect to the publication of the report. That I did in a telegram that I sent to him, and on which he acted. But that was not until after council had been informed.
I think my hon. friend the leader of the opposition was unfair in another particular. He -took a dispatch in the press which made certain adverse references to the circumstance that other developments had taken place over a
44	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
period of years which had now proved to be unwise, and he attributed what was in this newspaper' comment to my hon. friend, though the article itself commences with the words, "Mr. Dunning refused to make any comment on the matter whatever." I submit that my hon. friend could not have read that article as carefully as he should have done, for if he did. I do not believe he would have made the particular comment upon the action of the minister which, possibly, in a little haste, he did. So much for the Hudson Bay terminus and the motives that actuated the government in reference thereto.
My hon. friend spoke next of the transfer of the natural resources to Alberta, and rather regretted that there had been a considerable delay in making the transfer. May I say to my hon. friend that I join with him in the regret that these resources have not been transferred more speedily, though may I hasten to add this statement, that having had the advantage which the members of the government had of meeting in conference last November the premiers of the different provinces and their colleagues and of considering with them the question of the transfer of the natural resources to the western provinces, I feel that it is possibly fortunate for the province of Alberta, as well as for the other western provinces, that a decision has been deferred until the present time, and that the necessary legislation 'has not been passed up to the present moment.' Let me illustrate what I wish to convey.
One advantage of the conference was that premiers and ministers from the different provinces were in a position to give to the federal government an expression of opinion as to how in existing circumstances the action of the government would be viewed by their respective provinces-the action, for instance, of government with respect to subsidies to the maritime provinces under the Duncan report. We were pleased to find that without exception the premiers of the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, and of the western provinces, the premiers of all the provinces, were at one with the federal administration in having adopted the course which we did adopt in voting the grants which were made last session to the maritime provinces, and in saying that so far as their provinces were concerned they were only too happy that the maritimes should continue to be treated in like manner until at least the accounting which is asked for by the Duncan report had been completed. There was an evidence that the prairie provinces and British Columbia, as well as the central provinces, felt that in certain economic particulars the mari-
time provinces had been handicapped of recent years, and they were pleased that, as a factor contributing to the unity of our Dominion, the administration had taken the course it did in accordance with the recommendations of the Duncan report. Similarly in regard to the western provinces, we found, on the part of our friends from the maritimes, the premiers from Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, and also on the part of the premiers of Quebec and Ontario, a distinct willingness to have the federal government, in the matter of dealing with the prairie provinces, take what may be described as a generous attitude in so far as that was consistent with financial considerations of which the federal government has to take account. They seemed to feel that the government might well consider what, in arranging for the transfer of their resources to the prairie provinces, has been one of the main difficulties up to the present time, namely, the advisability of continuing, along with the return of the lands, the subsidies which up to the present time, had been paid in lieu of the lands. The moment that attitude on the part of the other provinces became apparent to the administration, we found we were in a position to negotiate with the prairie provinces on a basis much more satisfactory than had existed before we had received that general expression of view on the part of the other provinces of Canada. After all, while these are federal matters, they do also affect all the provinces in the Dominion. As a consequence of the discussion which took place at the conference, the government has reopened the subject of negotiations with the Premier of Alberta in regard to the return of the natural resources to that province, and I am authorized by the Premier of Alberta to inform this house that so far as he1 is concerned, these negotiations are proceeding in a manner that is satisfactory to him at the present time. I hope that that assurance, which means that the matter is being satisfactorily dealt with as wrell, so far as the federal administration is concerned, will quiet any alarm or misgivings which hon. members opposite may have, concerning the progress of negotiations regarding the transfer of the natural resources to Alberta.
Then I come to British Columbia, and there again the expression of views of the other provinces was helpful to the administration. British Columbia made strong representations why some of the lands in the railway belt and the Peace River block should be returned to the province. I confess that the government had anticipated the wish of the British

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
Columbia government in that matter by having an inquiry made. The late John Oliver, as hon. members know, repeatedly brought to the attention of the federal government what he claimed were the legal rights of the province of British Columbia in that matter. In the spring of last year, if I recollect aright, the government appointed Mr. Justice Martin as a royal commissioner to investigate the question of the legal claims of British Columbia in respect of these lands. Mr. Justice Martin has submitted to the government an interim report, in which 'he states that, while he does not think there are legal claims, he is of the opinion that there are strong claims in natural justice-claims in equity, so to speak, on the part of that province for the return of these lands. Mr. Justice Martin's final report is not yet in the hands of the government, but as soon as it is received it will be laid on the table of the 'house and no doubt hon. members will be guided in the matter of subsequent legislation by the findings which the commissioner may make. So much for the question of the natural resources.

What will be the policy
of the government in regard to the natural resources of Manitoba?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The same
policy in the matter of natural resources covers all the provinces of the west. The federal government believes that the natural resources of the western provinces should be returned to them, but there are questions in relation to the transfer which require to be carefully considered. I should not like in any way to see created a situation which would be embarrassing to either the federal or provincial governments where our action is intended to be one which will have the effect of removing embarrassment, and therefore we may be proceeding with a little more caution than we would otherwise.
In regard to the Duncan report, I am glad to see that hon. gentlemen opposite so cordially accept it in its findings, and speak so highly of the service which has been rendered by the commissioners in the making of their report. Let me remind them-and I do it in case by any chance they should repeat a criticism of the administration in adopting a similar method at another time-that when the government decided to have the question of the maritime claims referred to a commission we were told by some hon. gentlemen opposite-indeed the line of criticism of the opposition and particularly of members of the opposition who came from the maritime provinces was-that this was no sort of way to deal with the question, and that it was only a means of evading the responsibility of the government in respect thereto. It has turned out to be the opposite. The government at the present time has implemented a very considerable part of the report and we intend to continue to carry out its recommendations.
On the subject of scientific research, I think my hon. friend is at one with the government in its desire to see in this country the work of industrial and scientific reseach furthered as largely as may be possible, and in a manner which will lead to co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. There again may I say that the Dominion-provincial conference was extremely helpful'to the governments of the provinces as well as to the federal government. The subject was very fully discussed. The premiers of some of the provinces indicated the line on which they thought the provinces would be able most effectively to develop scientific research, and there was general agreement that, so far as the federal government was concerned, the establishment of laboratories here for the purpose of conducting certain lines of research would be the most important contribution which the Dominion could make. I will leave to my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce to inform the house at a later stage just what the intentions of the government are in that particular
My hon. friend has referred to the commission appointed to inquire into the fisheries of the maritime provinces in particular, and also of the province of Quebec, and has expressed the hope that its report will be tabled, so that hon. members may have it in the course of the present session. I will go one step further, and say that I hope that not only will the report be tabled, but that it may be tabled in time to permit this blouse, if thought desirable, to carry out in the form of legislation any of its recommendations, if legislation is called for.
Another matter to which my hon. friend referred was the announcement in the speech from the throne that the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and the Department of Health would be amalgamated in a new department under the title of National Health and Soldiers Welfare.
The leader of the opposition expressed surprise that the speech from the throne did not contain any further mention of the promise made last session of a committee to inquire into the question of pensions. Well, may I tell my hon. friend that if we had attempted to put into the speech from the throne all
46	[DOT] COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
that we intended or promised to do it would have been a much longer document than it is, and he might perhaps have criticized us on that score. But I hope he will not think that anything which has been left out of the speech from the throne in the nature of a promise made in a previous session is being overlooked. The government intends at the very earliest date to ask the house to appoint a special committee to consider legislation which will be brought down by the Minister of Health and Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment (Mr. King) and to recommend what may be advisable by way of amendment to existing legislation. The hope of the administration is that the committee will go very fully into the whole question of pensions in its bearing on the well-being and welfare of returned men.
The remaining part of the address of my hon. friend in relation to the speech from the throne which concerned domestic affairs had to do with the question of trade. I confess that listening to him yesterday and also reading with considerable interest the addresses which he has made since he became leader of his party, I have yet to learn exactly what he has in his mind as to the policy he thinks should be adopted by the government with respect to trade matters. I hope during the course of the session he will enlighten us, and, if his party has a policy with respect to trade, that he will give us some opportunity first of all of knowing what it is and, if it differs from our own, of debating the merits of it. Up to the present time he has told us that what this country needs more than anything else is the development of its natural resources, the expansion of its commerce, and the development of trade within the empire. Well, all these are matters of common agreement. Of course we want to develop, our natural resources, of course we want to trade with the different parts of the empire, and we want moreover to trade as widely as we can with all the countries of the world. If there is anything more than that in what my hon. friend has been telling the country is desirable in the way of policy, I hope he will enlighten us upon it.
I should like to ask him first of all, when he speaks of the development of our natural resources, whether in his experience of business affairs he has not found that capital is as necessary as labour in order to develop any branch of industry, particularly the great primary and manufacturing industries of the country. What the dominion needs at the present time is as much capital as possible brought in for the purpose of sound invest-

ment-not merely immigration for the purpose of supplying labour, but also the introduction of more capital. We want that capital from all quarters of the globe, and-may I say to my hon. friend?-the more we can get from the British Isles the happier we in this dominion will be. We cannot have too much British capital or British labour to develop our natural resources, so long as we are in a position properly to assimilate the population that comes to our shores; but simply to bring people into Canada without having the capital wherewith to put them to work in the development of our great primary industries is, I think, a questionable proceeding.
There are thirteen hundred and eighty-five million dollars of savings in this country not being used in industry or development. That is the answer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Does my hon. friend wish us to infer that he does not want any more capital to come in?

No. People are fearful
of using their capital. They are tying it up in the banks at three per cent instead of using it to develop industries.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would say
to my hon. friend that the large sums now in the banks is just another evidence of the great prosperity of this country. The more that is advertised to the world the more it will help to bring into this country the kind of settlers we want. I w'ould ask my hon. friend, as the leader of the party opposite, if, when he speaks on a subsequent occasion, he will be a little more explicit as to just exactly what he wants to see done in the way of trade development, and how that wider development is to be brought about. He has spoken a great deal about trade within the empire. I should like to ask him this question-not to reply to it immediately, but I hope during the session:	Does
he want free trade within the British Empire? Does he want an increase in the British preference; and if so, on what particular commodities? Does he wish us to trade only within the British Empire, to build up a sort of exclusive economic unit within the British Empire; or is he prepared to have the producers and manufacturers of this country buy and sell in as wide markets as it is possible for them to find? Before my hon. friend pretends to the country that he has a policy on trade matters T think he ought

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
to make clear first of all in his own mind what that policy is, and then give to us the benefit of a clear expression of his views.
Speaking of trade within the empire, I have a few figures here that may help my hon. friend to reach a decision on this matter of benefit to his party and himself. Let us take the figures with respect to trade with the United Kingdom and other parts of the British Empire. What are they? In 1896 we imported from the United Kingdom commodities to the value of $33,000,000; in 1926 our imports amounted, not to $33,000,000, but to $163,000,000. From other parts of the British Empire we imported $2,000,000 in 1896; that had grown to $44,000,000 in 1926. In other words, our total import trade with the British Empire had grown from $35,000,000 in 1896 to $207,000,000 in 1926. Our exports to the United Kingdom in 1896 totalled $62,000,000; in 1926 that total had reached the large figure of $513,000,000. To other parts of the British Empire we exported in 1896 $4,000,000, and in 1926 $85,000,000. In other words, our total exports to the British Empire increased from $66,000,000 in 1896 to $598,000,000 in 1926.
While that is an enormous growth of trade within the British Empire and one of which we are all proud, may I draw my hon. friend's attention to this fact: that while in 1896 the empire took 60 per cent of our exports, in 1926 it took only 45 per cent, although there had been that great expansion from $66,000,000 to $598,000,000 in the total exports from this Dominion to the various parts of the empire. That, it seems to me, means that if this Dominion is to find markets for its produce and products, whether they be the raw materials that my hon. friend speaks of so much, or the goods that are manufactured from them, those markets must be found in all parts of the world. The United Kingdom or the British Empire as a whole cannot begin to take from us all the commodities we have to sell. Are we to wait until my hon. friend has brought about this economic union which he speaks of in a theoretical way in order that we may trade within the empire to the exclusion of other parts of the world?
He did not say that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I may be
wrong in interpreting what my hon. friend has in mind, but I think the house will agree with me that he has been sailing pretty close to the idea of a sort of economic unit of trade within the British Empire.
But he did not say it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am glad to have got that much from my hon. friend, that he has never said that we are to seek to make an economic unit of the British Empire in the matter of trade. However, may I make our position clear: What we want first of all is trade, and we would prefer to have that trade in largest measure within the empire. Wherever, therefore, there is opportunity for trade we shall take advantage of it, first of all among ourselves at home and next, other things being equal, with other parts of the empire, in preference to trading beyond. But when we have gone as far as we can in developing trade among ourselves and within the empire, then, if it is to the economic interests of the citizens of the Dominion to find other markets, we shall endeavour as far as we can to obtain such markets, and the best markets possible, in all parts of the world.
Let me call my hon. friend's attention to what appeals to me as an important consideration in this matter. What do we mean by raw material? The grain that is grown in the field is raw material: it is raw material from which flour is subsequently manufactured. Are we to understand that Canada is not to export her wheat at all but only to manufacture it into flour, shipping out the finished product alone? Flour itself is in turn a raw material, used in the making of bread. Are we therefore to cease exporting our flour and to export only bread? And so we might pursue the query? Take newsprint, for example: newsprint comes from pulp and pulp, as my hon. friend knows, is a product of the trees of the forest. But newsprint is a raw material; it is used for a variety of purposes. It beoomes therefore a question whether we shall stop exporting newsprint, if the argument that is advanced is to be regarded as sound. If that is to be the case, let me remind hon. members that we have reached in Canada to-day the point where we have not only the greatest record which this country has ever achieved in the export of wheat and newsprint, but that our record in respect of the export of these two commodities is also the greatest of any country in the world. It seems to me further, we should keep in mind, if we are to have a proper appreciation of matters of this sort, the significance of conservation-something which my hon. friend apparently disregards altogether. Because wheat is grown and exported one year it does not follow that the soil has been exhausted and is incapable of
48	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
repeating the same reproductive process year in and year out. If proper regard is had for the rotation of crops, and for other considerations of which agriculturists 'have a wide knowledge, there is no reason why the fecundity of nature should not continue from year to year with increasing advantage to the nation. Similarly with regard to our forests. My hon. friend in some of his utterances seems occasionally to be under the delusion that we are necessarily depleting the country of its forests when we export such large quantities of newsprint. There again he should consider the importance of conservation properly carried on as a means of restoring and renewing our forests. If my hon. friend will give due consideration to this aspect I am sure that many doubts he may have in the matter will be removed.
I pass now to the next subject which the bon. leader of the opposition touched upon, namely, immigration. Here again I find the same difficulty in appreciating what precisely he has in mind. If he will scan the remarks he made in the house yesterday, as reported, he will see that what he suggested was the introduction of some immense scheme in relation to immigration. Apparently he seemed to think that the country was dissatisfied with the restrictive measures at present in force and that what was most needed was some large policy that would involve a considerable expenditure. If that is what he contemplates, I wish he would tell us just what the scheme is. That is what we are entitled to know. What does be want to initiate? What does he want to do with the money which he wishes parliament to vote for immigration? Does he want it spent in bringing into the country people to work in the factories? If so, let him tell us. Does he want to bring in people indiscriminately, without any of the restrictions that exist at the present time? If that is what he has in mind, should he not so inform the House? But do not let him criticize the government's immigration policy simply on the score of its not being satisfactory because it is not large enough to satisfy some ambition which he himself has not seen fit to disclose to the country.
As to the government's immigration policy, let me say this-and if this is not going far enough I wish my hon. friend would suggest how much further we ought to go-our policy is to bring into the country just as many people, of proper physique and general qualifications, as the country is capable of assimilating with satisfaction to itself as well as to those who are brought in. We do not wish to bring into Canada races that are not assimil-
* Mr. Mackenzie King. 1
able. We do not wish to bring in peoples from countries that have populations which, as experience has shown, do not make good citizens or settlers in our dominion. On the other hand, wherever men and women of strong, healthy physique and of proper character can be found, the doors of the country are open to receive them, under such restrictions only as this parliament places, or authorizes the government to place, upon their entrance into Canada. Parliament in its wisdom has thought well to make a distinction between different classes coming into Canada. We have felt that as a British dominion we should welcome, in larger measure than from any other country, immigrants from the British Isles. It is the desire and the wish of the administration to encourage as largely as we can immigration from England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales. We want to build up this part of the British Empire with people of British stock. But if the British Isles are not prepared to send their people, if the people of the British Isles do not wish to emigrate' to this country, despite the inducements we offer, then we feel called upon, in the endeavour to increase the population of this dominion by immigration, to introduce strange stocks from other countries as well. The policy, then, is to accept as the best stocks, next to the people of the British Isles, those who come from the northern races of Europe, not because we have any particular criticism to make of the individuals who come from the southern climes of Europe, but because experience has shown that the northern stocks are best adapted to this northern half of North America. The effort of the department is to encourage immigration of people from Norway, Sweden, Denmark and other northern countries, next after those of the British Isles.
There are certain parts of Europe from which it has been thought advisable not to seek to bring in immigrants to any large extent, and parliament has decided that they shall be permitted to come in only subject to special permission on the part of the minister or of the department. My hon. friend said yesterday, with respect to permits, that all sorts of rumours were afloat regarding the department. He intimated that there was suspicion and a feeling that people were being kept out who should be allowed to come in, and that there was need for investigation. I am very glad that he made reference to this matter, because I think that wherever there is suspicion abroad the sooner we know about it the better; the sooner the whole matter is investigated the better it will be for everyone concerned.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
Let me say to the house that the officials of the department have an extremely difficult task to perform. In the matter of administration they are restricted by the obligations which parliament imposes upon them; and, on the other hand, they have to stand all the abuse that may be directed against them for not meeting the wishes of persons who, from [DOT] one motive or another, hold a view different from that which parliament has decided should prevail. I remember being much impressed in this house on one occasion with a remark made by the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, to the effect that not only every member of the government 'but, as well, every member of parliament owed a special duty to the civil service to uphold public servants who endeavoured to discharge their duties honourably and honestly. The government of the country is carried on by a large body of civil servants who act under instructions and in accordance with the policies laid down by parliament. They are not free agents; if they did as they pleased they would be violating the obligations of their positions. They are put in positions and are expected to administer the law in accordance with the provisions of the statute. The Deputy Minister of the Department of Immigration, Mr. Egan, has sought, I believe, to administer the affairs of his department honestly. He is fearless and courageous, and all that I have seen of him makes me believe that he is possessed of the qualities which it is desirable to have in officers of the public service. If Mr. Egan is restricting immigrants from coming into this country in consequence of any regulation, all I have to say is it is for parliament to decide whether that regulation should continue or not. So long as the regulation is there, and the officer seeks only to uphold the regulation, no member of parliament is entitled to criticize him adversely. If there is any criticism to be made let it be directed against the government that keeps the officer in his present .position. Let me say to my hon. friend that the government will be only too happy to have all the affairs of the Department of Immigration discussed and investigated by a committee of this house during the present session. It is suggested that that committee should be the committee on agriculture and colonization. I think that possibly, in view of its membership, it is the best committee to investigate matters relating to the Department of Immigration. I know that the minister at the head of the department was quick to volunteer the statement that he would welcome the fullest investigation into the affairs of the department, by the members of the committee. That investigation can easily be arranged, and will be arranged during the course of the present session.
My hon. friend stated that there was sus- [DOT] picion as to the permits that were being issued, as to how they were being issued and the like. May I say that if it is found that permits are being issued in an illegal manner no time will be lost on the part of the administration in seeing that that procedure is brought to an end very summarily. I wish to say, because it is within my own certain knowledge, that members on both sides are coming to the Minister of Immigration from day to day and pleading for the right to have permits granted to certain people in their own constituencies. That is known to every hon. member, and I say that if hon. gentlemen do not wish the permit system to continue by all means let it be discontinued. But if the permit system is regarded by parliament as wise, I would urge hon. members to support the minister and the department in their efforts to carry out that system properly.
I am not so sure that the views expressed by my hon. friend in regard to the extent of immigration to Canada give a fair idea of what is being done. My hon. friend expressed the view that we were doing nothing at all, and that immigration was being brought almost to a standstill. The hon. gentleman knows better than that. Not only is that the case, but his own words disclose that he knows directly the opposite, because elsewhere in his address he said that there were not half of those that came in 1913. My hon. friend chose 1913 because it was the peak year, so to speak, of the immigration movement to Canada. Let me point out that 1913 was before the war. At that time Europe was in a state of panic, and many people were trying to get away from the continent as fast as they could. In 1913 transportation costs across the Atlantic were low. These were factors which contributed to a heavy immigration movement at that time. Moreover, for a number of years previous to 1913 there had been considerable immigration from Europe to Canada, and as every hon. member knows no immigration propaganda is as effective and as helpful as that which comes from immigrants who have come to this country and are living here happily and contented. They are glad then to induce their friends to come and settle in the new land where they themselves have encountered success. I need not point out the unfairness in making a comparison between 1913 and to-day. Take the population of Europe to-day. Why that continent has been largely depopulated of those progressive spirits who



The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
are ready to move from one part of the world to another when opportunity offers. There is no country in Europe, and that is true particularly of the British Isles, which has not suffered a tremendous loss of manhood in consequence of the war. How then is it possible to get the same volume of immigration that took place in 1913 and preceding years. In 1913-I speak only from memory at the moment-my impression is that you could go from ports in the British Isles to Montreal for something like $25 or less. To-day the fare is $80 or more. That is a very different situation to-day when we want to get immigrants. Notwithstanding the handicap to which I have alluded the immigration to Canada for the first nine months of the last fiscal year amounted to 128,928 persons, an increase over the corresponding period of 1926 of 14,893, or 13 per cent. Of the total of 128,928 the immigration of British, United States, French, Belgian, Swiss, Scandinavian, Dutch or German origin amounted to 92,955. In the nine months under review-here I want to direct the attention of the house to a statement by my hon. friend that Canadians were leaving the west to go into the United States-33,722 Canadians returned to live in Canada from the United States where they had gone with the declared intention of residing there permanently.

Is the Prime Minister
aware that in the last five years more Canadians crossed to the United States than the number of immigrants who, from all sources, came to this country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am not, but I would say this to my hon. friend. I would rather in the interests of immigration give to the country the statement I have just made than the one he has made to the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: "Whisper of death."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is insinuated sometimes that the government is not doing as much as it should towards encouraging immigration from the British Isles as compared with Europe. What are the facts? I will ask hon. members to listen for a moment while I communicate the details of the relative expenditure on bringing immigrants to Canada from the British Isles as compared with bringing them from Europe, and ask if they think the insinuation or implication is correct that we are doing more for immigration from Europe than we are for immigration from the British Isles. The expenditures on the continent of Europe totalled $63,000 in 1925-26, and $57,000 in 1926-27. The per capita cost of continental immigrants 
was approximately $1.50 in 1926 and less than 80 cents in 1927. In the British Isles during 1925-26 we spent in advertising, literature, exhibitions and general office expenses, $427,000, and on passage assistance during the same period, $317,000, a total of $744,000, or an average of approximately $20 for every British immigrant secured. In 1926-27 the expenditure was $881,000, or an average of something over $17 per capita. For the continental immigrant there is no passage assistance; he pays a minimum ocean rate of $112.50 or stays at home. A Britisher who pays his own way pays a minimum ocean rate of $84.50, while if he belongs to the classes receiving assisted passages, his ocean passage costs him but two pounds and his children under seventeen years of age travel free.
That is the position as between the continent and Britain and I submit that those figures are unanswerable as to the effort on the part of the government to encourage migration from Great Britain. WThen my hon. friend speaks about other parts of the empire receiving British immigrants, what are the figures? In the calendar year 1927 Canada received 47,607, Australia 27,571 immigrants. During the same period there was a total of 60,967 passages assisted in England, of which Canada received 29,287, Australia 26,021, New Zealand 5,368 and South Africa 293. Therefore our proportion of immigrants from the British Isles who received assisted passages was the largest of any of the dominions. One would think, from much that one reads in the press, that Australia and other countries were getting away ahead of us in British immigrants. My hon. friend, I think, will discover when the committee on agriculture and colonization considers this question, that what is really at the back of all this criticism of the Department of Immigration is the fact that while this parliament is prepared to vote money to assist immigrants to come to Canada who will take up agriculture as an occupation or become domestic servants, parliament is not prepared to vote money for persons who will engage in other occupations and callings.
Those who are interested in bringing into this country people regardless of the occupation into which they will go are continually finding fault with the administration because our assisted passages are limited to those two classes and because equal amounts are not given to people who wish to enter Canada to engage in other occupations. I ask hon. gentlemen opposite who are members of the legal and medical professions how long thev

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
would tolerate a contribution by the state to bring in by assisted passages lawyers and doctors in large numbers from the British Isles to Canada. The man who is a mechanic working at his trade, the skilled engineer, the miner, men in the building trades and the like feel in exactly the same way with respect to what they have devoted of their time and energy in acquiring skill in their particular trades.

In respect of those other
than agriculturists who are coming in, is it not a fact that they are prevented from coming in from other countries than Great Britain unless they go into agriculture or become domestic servants?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think my
hon. friend is mistaken there in the broad inference that one would take from his remarks. May I .put the matter in this way? As regards the British Isles anyone can come to this country who can qualify as being physically fit; there is no restriction of any kind. As regards Europe there is an occupational test; a man has to follow a particular occupation in order to be permitted to enter Canada as an immigrant. May I add this further? As regards the British Isles, if the immigrant belongs to the agriculturist class or is a domestic servant his or her passage is assisted, paid for the most part by the state. In connection with Britain there is further a contribution by this parliament which is j oined in by the parliament of Great Britain towards the settlement of families from the British Isles in this country. That does not exist with respect to the continent.
There are some European countries from which certain classes, as I indicated a moment ago, can come only under special permission. But parliament has decided that, and the Department of Immigration is surely not to be blamed for carrying out regulations which parliament has made. If hon. gentlemen feel that we should not exclude any class from Europe, all they have to do is to amend the law to that effect. But I submit that they will not do so because what in the matter of immigrants is of greatest importance to this Dominion looking to the future is quality rather than quantity.

I am asking purely for information and not from any partisan motives. Is it possible under the regulations for a citizen of France, no matter how wealthy he may be, who is engaged in any occupation 56103-41	,
except that of agriculture or domestic service, to enter Canada at the present time for the purpose of settling?

I might answer for the
Prime Minister. As a matter of actual practice, immigrants from all countries of northern Europe are coming in under practically the same provisions as immigrants from Great Britain provided that they pass the health qualifications.

If they get special permits
from the minister.
No.

A relative of mine who
happened to be a French citizen came into Canada to stay for six months, and although
a person of wealth and distinction I was asked to give a bond for return.
If the hon. member will give me the name of that person I will make inquiry and I will guarantee that the case is not exactly as he states.
My statement will stand.
I will take the name.
Does the Prime Minister not think the farmer has the same right to object to competition as the doctor or the lawyer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have no doubt he has the same right to object but he does not do so. The farmer is anxious to get as much as he can in the way of agricultural assistance land I ithink he takes a much broader view on these questions than some others.

May I direct my right
hon. friend's attention to the fact that it is not the statute that prohibits but the regulations made by order in council under the statute and this parliament has not had an opportunity of dealing with the matter, but rather orders in council prepared by the government have been made to conform to particular eases that are desired to be met.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am quite
prepared to agree with my hon. friend that the statute gives the government authority to make regulations. Those regulations are laid on the table of the house; they are known to all hon. members. If those regulations are not satisfactory, let us have a debate on the matter and amend and change them. The point that I am making at the moment is that as long as those regulations exist it is unfair to officials of the department who are doing their utmost to serve their

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
country faithfully and well, to criticise them on the score that they are endeavouring to restrict and prevent people from coming into Canada. My hon. friend said that he had a telegram from some friend of his in Europe complaining about instructions with respect to medical examination.
From London.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That serves to illustrate just how far criticism may go in completely misrepresenting the intention and purpose of the administration in respect of some of the so-called regulations. For years the medical examination of immigrants to Canada took place on this side of the ocean. I think hon. members will all agree that we do not want in this country classes who are defective, delinquent and dependent, but that we want classes that will come up to a certain qualification. The examination took place at Grosse lie, with what result? The result was that many of those who had left their homes in the old country were turned back when they reached the shores of Canada. What was the criticism made? The criticism was that the government by making its examinations on this side was deterring immigration; that every man who was sent back became a centre of discontent in the country to which he returned. It was urged that instead of having these examinations made at the time of landing and consequent painful returns of immigrants to the old country, the examination should be made in the old country itself. Then at great expense, because it is a great expense, the government appointed medical examiners in Europe and the British Isles, placing them not one in every village but at a considerable number of points. Now we are criticized because of alleged extravagance by the government in paying for these physicians on the other side, and then our hon. friend comes and tells us that we are criticized because we make the immigrants on the other side undergo this examination.
No; it is the character of the examination.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
This also is a matter which I would wish this committee to discuss, and I think it will be shown that every one of the so-called restrictions has been made primarily if not entirely in the interests of the immigrant. As I say, I believe it will serve a useful purpose in every direction to have the entire question of immigration as thoroughly ventilated as possible.
WTith respect to the empire settlement scheme, and in particular to the possible criticism that we are not doing as much as we fMr. Mackenzie Kin i.l
should, may I quote a paragraph from an interview given at Vancouver by the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, Mr. Amery, in regard to this government's part in cooperating with the British government in empire settlement? As every hon. member knows, no one has more at heart than Mr. Amery, the -Secretary of State for the Dominions, the success of the empire settlement scheme. Here is what Mr. Amery said in one of his first interviews:
I do not think there is any feeling in Great Britain that the Canadian government is not doing its part to stimulate immigration, and I do not think there has been any apathy on the part of the Canadian government in the old land in this respect. The fact is there have been economic factors at work which have retarded the flow of emigration to this country.
There is a statement which I hope hon. members will take as authoritative having regard to the source which I have mentioned.
I regret that I have found it necessary to dwell at such length on these matters of immediate domestic concern. I shall endeavour speedily to conclude by referring to the two other main subjects which my hon. friend brought up in his address. I refer to imperial and international questions.
First of all, may I allude to the remarks of my hon. friend on the alleged commitments of our country at the League of Nations. He said, if I followed him aright, that parliament ought to know a great deal more about what is going on at the League of Nations and what we are being committed to than it does; that there has been recently an economic commission on which Canada has been represented, and that the implications of its findings are matters of concern to all of us, and he said that these commissions should not exist without a fuller knowledge on the part of members of this house as to what they are doing. He also intimated, in particular, that there was an order in council or a despatch sent some time ago which set out the policy of the government in regard to arbitration; or rather, it was the other way round- that the policy of the government in regard to arbitration in international affairs was a matter on which he desired to have more concrete information, and which he thought- my hon. friend shakes his head. Did I not understand him aright?

I referred to the observations with respect to Senator Dandurand's speech, and I said that in my judgment that speech did not warrant the implications founded upon it. My right hon. friend will find what I said in Hansard.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Probably there is very little difference between my hon. friend and myself on this point. The government's policy with respect to arbitration was set out in a despatch tabled two years ago. What I wish to say *with respect to the League of Nations and the part that this country is assuming in relation thereto is this:	As hon. members of the house know,
the reports of the representatives of this country at the League of Nations, the reports of delegates who have been appointed to the league, are tabled every session, and in addition to that, there is distributed to all members of parliament the proceedings of the League of Nations which contain, I understand, all that transpires there that is of moment. These documents give as complete information to members of the house as it is possible to get from any source.
In regard to the economic commission to which my hon. friend has just referred, may I say to him at once and to the house that that was not a commission on which ministers of the crown were represented. It committed the government or the country to nothing. It was a commission of experts on economic questions, meeting under the auspices of the League of Nations to discuss means of more effectively bringing about greater stability in economic matters throughout the world-a body of experts who met in Geneva and discussed these matters there, and prepared a report. That report will be presented to parliament. The report of our members on the economic commission will be presented to parliament, I hope, to-morrow. It would have been ready for presentation to-day, but it is being translated. I desired to present both the French and English copies at the same time.
I now come to that part of my hon. friend's address which touches upon the much discussed subject of status. May I say to the leader of the opposition at once that so far as we on this side of the. house are concerned, our view in regard to Canada's position within the British Empire is none other than that which was laid down at the Imperial conference of 1926, in that part of the report of the conference which relates to the status of Great Britain and the dominions and which is set forth in black and white in the published proceedings of that body. May I say this further to him, that in that particular, namely, in our view as to Canada's position, we do not differ one whit from the view of the government of Great Britain, the government of New Zealand, the government of South
Africa, the government of Newfoundland, and the government of the Irish Free State. All the governments of the self-governing dominions, and the government of the mother country have expressed their view as to the present constitutional position of the dominions and the mother country, and that position is the position which we at all events, as the Liberal party in this country and, in another capacity, as the government of this country, take with respect to Canada's status at the present time. May I read from the proceedings of the imperial conference the exact statement of Canada's position as we conceive it to be in relation to other parts of the British Empire? The report of the conference reads:
There is, however, one most important element in it-the British Empire-which, from a strictly constitutional point of view, has now', as regards all vital matters, reached its full development-we refer to the group of selfgoverning communities composed of Great Britain and the dominions. Their position and mutual relation may be readily defined. They are autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status, in no wray subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the crown, and freely associated as members of the British commonwealth of nations.
That position has not only been emphasized, as my hon. friend has said, by my colleague the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and myself and other members of the government, but it has been stressed in this country by every visitor we have had in this Dominion in the past year who has had anything to do with the imperial conference. The Prime Minister of Australia, when he passed through Canada, said that this was the position so far as Australia was concerned in regard to its relations to the other parts of the empire.

Australia can amend its
own constitution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am going
to have a word with my hon. friend on that point in a moment. Then the Premier of New Zealand took the same position as respects both New Zealand and Canada. We have just had a visit from the President of the Executive Council of the Irish Free State, who has taken exactly the same position, and we have had within the last week a visit from the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs who has repeated at different points in this country the same position. We had during the summer a visit from the Prime Minister of Great Britain, not to

My hon. friend has just interjected that Australia has the power to amend its own constitution. What I wish he would tell the house is whether, if he is in any way dissatisfied with the present arrangement, he is prepared to join with us in having amended the present procedure in regard to the amending of our constitution.

The responsibility rests
at the moment with my right hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend says that the responsibility rests with us at the moment. Under the circumstances, and since he hesitates to give expression to his own view, let me give to the House what I conceive to be the views and desires of my hon. friend with regard to the amending of our constitution. I think that possibly my hon. friend and those of us who sit on this side of the house are not very far apart on this matter. At all events we were not very far apart before he became the leader of his party, and I cannot believe he has changed since, although no doubt he has received warnings from those who sit about him as to how far he should go in these matters. I have in my hand a copy of a very admirable address which my hon. friend delivered before the board of trade of his native city, Calgary, on June 5, 1927, before he had become the leader of his party. May I just read to the house the account which appears in his own paper, the Albertan, of the address which he delivered there?

To those who live in

If Canada is to be a nation she must have this power. In its ultimate analysis the constitution of Canada is a statute passed by Great Britain. The British parliament is supreme except in cases where it has delegated its power,
