speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend must leave the house to judge from this just what his real desire with respect to nationhood is.

I did suggest-and that is a very casual report in the newspaper-that it was highly desirable that the young men of this country should think in terms of the possible amendment of our constitution, and with respect to the flag-it was the time of the controversy in South Africa when the people were tied up with that problem-I said it was time the people of this country were thinking of it. I do not withdraw a single word of what I said.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Yesterday in the course of my hon. friend's remarks, he used the word " implication " and spoke of what was implied. It is desirable that the house should know just what his point of view is with respect to the position of Canada
within the empire and what deduction is to be drawn from his own utterances in this regard.
I will not take up the time of the house by citing statements of other parties as to Canada's position, but I would like to put on record one statement made by Mr. Amery, Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, who is here in our country, with respect to what, in his opinion, was laid down at the conference. Speaking as a British minister he said:
The conference had laid down in the first place the complete equality of British nations-* that none was subordinated to another. "Canada is no more subordinate to Britain than Britain is to Canada" he declared. "That principle is laid down for the whole empire with absolute unanimity."
With that statement we on this side of the house are in entire accord and complete agreement.
Yesterday my hon. friend's remarks were directed in large part to the Colonial Laws Validity Act, and he argued that because there is on the statute books of Great Britain a law known as the Colonial Laws Validity Act, under which statutes repugnant to the laws of Great Britain when passed by this parliament become of no force and effect, we are not, shall I say, a nation-
Not of equal status.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Not of equal
status with the mother country. May I say to my hon. friend that if he is speaking of purely legal technicalities-
Not technicalitiesofficial interpretation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Legal interpretation-then perhaps he can find some support for what he says, but may I remind him that every recognized authority on constitutional law and constitutional history has taken the view that the constitution is something larger and broader and higher and deeper than a mere matter of law. The constitution is not made of statutes alone, but of customs and practices and traditions, as he well knows, and of principles and practices which have been long in use, all of which played their part in determining the constitutional position and status of a country.

I desire to make myself
perfectly clear to my right hon. friend. I say the customs and practices have nothing whatever to do with judicial interpretations. The courts take no notice of anything else but statutes, as appears in the Nadan case, and therefore in the Nadan case they interpreted the statutes- -

The Andress-Mr. Mackenzie King

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not wish to go into the legal side of this matter with my hon. friend. I prefer to leave that to the legal members of the house. But I want to say that there would be some force in his contention if the factor to which he has drawn our attention had not been the very factor of which full notice had been taken and to which particular consideration had been given at the conference. What was the precise endeavour of the conference with regard to describing the status of the dominion? It was, first of all, to discover whether there was agreement between all parts of the British Empire as to the nature of the relations existing between the different self-governing parts to each other; and if so, what the basic principle of the relationship was. There was no difficulty in discovering that. It was agreed by all that it had been a matter of evolution. It was not some new thing of the moment, brought for the first time into being. It was the opinion of all that the point reached in the constitutional evolution of the dominions themselves and their relation to the governments of Great Britain and of one another was such that the only accurate description of the relationship existing between them was one of equality of status. Once that principle had been laid down, then the conference proceeded to see whether in any particular there was a survival of the old order which had passed away. It was recognized that there had been a change. I submit that the greatest of all the transformations that had taken place in respect to the British Empire had been the transformation from the conception of the empire as an imperial unit to be highly developed in the form of a federation to this acknowledged conception of the empire as a community of free nations, owing a common allegiance to the same crown, having similar constitutions, cooperating with one another in accordance with certain well understood principles, but in no state of subordination one to the other.
Having laid down the position, the conference had then, as I have said, to see whether there were survivals of the old order, whether there were anachronisms, whether there remained anomalies. As was to be expected, one, two, three or four anomalies presented themselves. One was the case my hon. friend has mentioned. If you have equality of status, if that is the position between the dominions and the mother country, how can you reconcile that equality of status with the power which the Colonial Laws Validity Act apparently gives to the imperial parliament?
(Mr. Bermett.]
That is what is troubling my hon. friend. It was noticed at once at the conference that that was an anomaly; at once it was stressed that the statute could not continue to be operative under the condition which has now come to be recognized, and immediately the conference undertook to provide ways and means of removing that anomaly. Instead of seeking to remove it instantly during the sessions of a conference which had been called only for a few weeks, and which was then nearing its close, recognizing that there were legal obligations and difficulties involved, it was decided that a committee of experts from different parts of the empire would meet with a view of considering how that particular anomaly might be removed before the time of or at a subsequent conference.
The whole position in that regard has been set out in the proceedings of the conference. Let me, in order to confirm what I have said, read from the text of the report of the conference. After setting forth the statement of equality of status in the terms in which I have read it, the report has the following:
Equality of status, so far as Britain and the dominions are concerned, is thus the root principle governing our inter-imperial relations. But the principles of equality and similarity, appropriate to status, do not universally extend to function.
I do not need to continue on that part.
It is puzzling to me to know what "function" means.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend and I will have to talk about that some evening. I think we can work it out together. Here is .the point:
Existing administrative, legislative, and judicial forms-
My hon. friend has referred to the judiciary; there is a reference to judicial forms.
-are admittedly not wholly in accord with the position as described in section 2 of this report.
The conference recognized that there were some features not in accord with the principle.
This is inevitable, since most of these forms date back to a time well antecedent to the present stage of constitutional development. Our first task then was to examine these forms with special reference to any cases where the want of adaptation of practice to principle caused, or might be thought to cause, inconvenience in the conduct of inter-imperial relations.
Going on from that stage in the procedure, under the head of Operation of Dominion Legislation, the report continues as follows:

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
Our attention was also called to various points in connection with the operation of dominion legislation which, it was suggested, required clarification.
And what was one of those points?
(d) The operation of legislation passed by the parliament at Westminster in relation to the dominions. In this connection special attention was called to such statutes as the Colonial Laws Validity Act.
The very point that my hon. friend has drawn our attention to. Now what does the report continue to say with regard to that?
We gave these matters the best consideration possible in the limited time at our disposal, but came to the conclusion that the issues involved were so complex that there would be grave danger in attempting any immediate pronouncement other than a statement of certain principles which, in our opinion, underlie the whole question of the operation of dominion legislation.
What is said further on this point?
Is not that an ideal to be attained rather than a realization at the present time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite correct in saying, it is an ideal to be attained, and I hope he will join me in the endeavour to bring about its attainment.
There is no pretence of our having attained it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is no pretence; this statement sets the situation forth in black and white. This citation, .1 think, answers what my hon. friend says about "pretence". Referring to certain matters that may have to be considered in the interim the report says:
On this point we propose that it should be placed on record that apart from provisions embodied in constitutions or in specific statutes expressly providing for reservation, it is recognized that it is the right of the government of each dominion to advise the crown in all matters relating to its own affairs. Consequently, it would not be in accordance with constitutional practice for advice to be tendered to His Majesty by His Majesty's government in Great Britain on any matter pertaining to the affairs of a dominion against the views of the government of that dominion.
Now, Mr. Speaker, when the British government itself declares that with respect to any statute which affects this dominion it will not undertake to advise His Majesty, but will have His Majesty advised by the government of this dominion, whether it be with respect to the Colonial Laws Validity Act or any other statute, I submit that we need have no fear about the full establishment of the principle of equality of status as between governments. Then the report goes on to say that:
Steps should be taken by Great Britain and the dominions to set up a committee with terms of reference on the following lines:-
And one reference is:
(iii) The principles embodied in or underlying the Colonial Laws Validity Act, 1865, and the extent to which any provisions of that act ought to be repealed amended or modified in the light of the existing relations between the various members of the British Commonwealth of Nations as described in this report.
May I suggest to my hon. friend that perhaps he would be well advised to give to this particular question the same degree of thought that his predecessor in the high office which he now holds as leader of the Conservative party has given to it. I think he will find if he reads what Sir Robert Borden has written on the question of status that Sir Robert takes as to the evolution in the constitutional development of the Dominion very much the view which is now being expressed. May I cite one paragraph from Sir Robert's treatise on Canadian Constitutional Studies which relates to the question of Canadian status. Probably we will hear my hon. friend quoting it one day on a Conservative platform as a part of his policy:
As no formal attempt was made to define the constitutional relations between the British and Canadian governments, those relations were free to develop by the same slow and sure steps which had built up the system of government now obtaining in the United Kingdom. Unfettered by a written constitution in the ordinary acceptation of the term, that system has been moidded and is controlled by custom and convention to a remarkable extent. In the words of Lord Bryce, "the always changing constitution becomes interpenetrated by custom." Anson puts it in much the same way: "If in our constitution we find that law and custom diverge, we must note first what is the law, and then how it has been overgrown by custom."
"The conventions are superimposed upon the law, and modify political relations without in the least affecting legal ones." In an interesting contribution to the history and study of relations between the nations of the British commonwealth, Mr. H. Duncan Hall points out the vast scope of changes that may be effected through new conventions of the constitution.
Since then we have had the Nadan decision.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend, with all his legal acumen, might well, instead of seeking to emphasize a small technical point upon which he dwells at such length, offer the house some advice as to how best, for the benefit of all concerned to remove this last anachronism, this trifling anomaly, this irritating remnant.
And now may I conclude by referring to the one other matter in the speech from the throne which my hon. friend discussed at some length,
,	.	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
namely, the decision on the part of the administration to have ministers plenipotentiary exchanged between France and Canada and between Japan and Canada. May I here preface what I have to say by reading the paragraph which appears in the speech from the throne. I would ask hon. members to follow the sequence of statements as they are there set forth. The paragraph in the speech from the throne reads:
As contemplated by the conclusions of the imperial conference of 1926, provision was made on July 1 for direct communication between . His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's other governments of the British Empire. The further implementing of these conclusions which aim at more effective consultation through personal contact by the appointment to Canada of a representative of His Majesty's government in Great Britain is being discussed between the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs in Great Britain, who is at present in Canada, and members of my government. By agreement between the governments of France and Canada and the governments of Japan and Canada it is proposed that each of these countries shall be represented in the other by a minister plenipotentiary.
Let me now take the proceedings of the Imperial conference as they relate to the question of representation between Great Britain and Canada and indicate to the house what was there agreed upon among the representatives. At page 22 of the report, under the heading, System of Communication and Consultation, there appears the following:
Sessions of the imperial conference at which the Prime Ministers of Great Britain and of the dominions are all able to be present cannot, from the nature of things, take place very frequently. The system of communication and consultation between conferences becomes therefore of special importance. We reviewed the position now reached in this respect, with special reference to the desirability of arranging that closer personal touch should be established between Great Britain and the dominions, and the dominions inter se. Such contact alone can convey an impression of the atmosphere in which official correspondence is conducted. Development in this respect seems particularly necessary in relation to matters of major importance in foreign affairs, where expedition is often essential and urgent decision necessary. A special aspect of the question of consultation which we considered was that concerning the representation of Great Britain in the dominions. By reason of his constitutional position, as explained in section 4	(b) of this report, the Governor
General is no longer the representative of His Majesty's government in Great Britain. There is no one therefore in the dominion capitals in a position to represent with authority the views of His Majesty's government in Great Britain.
That is all I need quote in the present connection. What I wish to direct the attention of the house to is this: The Imperial confer-

enice, composed of those members of the several governments within the empire who have to do for the most part with communications passing between different parts of the empire, were agreed that the time had come when there should be not only direct communication as between government and government but also greater opportunity provided by way of personal contact and personal consultation, as a supplement to the written words of a despatch exchanged between governments. Perhaps I might state it thus wise: As nations, in their relations one with another, have found it advisable as the years have passed, to develop a diplomatic service whereby communications may be exchanged not merely in the form of written despatches from one government to another but having the advantages of personal contacts as well, so within the British Empire, with the business of the empire growing as it is, and with the increasing need for cooperation, extending as it has extended since the war, a useful purpose will be served if, in addition to written despatches, there are resident in the various capitals within the empire personal representatives from other parts of the British commonwealth of nations. It was recognized that it was for each dominion and for the British government to decide individually how best it should be represented in the other self-governing communities. Canada has been represented in London for many yearn by a High Commissioner. The High Commissioner in London holds the highest position in the gift of this government in its diplomatic relations with the world outside Canada. As between the other governments of the British Empire and Canada on the one hand, and as between foreign countries and Canada on the other, there is of necessity a considerable difference income particulars in the matter of representation. lit seems to me that there must be drawn a distinct line between representation as between units within the empire and the representation of a dominion in foreign countries. I believe that so long as there is a British Empire the contacts within the empire will be to each dominion more important, more numerous, in every particular more essential, than will be the relation between that dominion and any foreign country; and for that reason I shall always feel that, so far as this country is concerned, the highest post in a representative capacity that may be given beyond the 'Confines of Canada will be the post occupied by the official, whoever he may be, representing this Dominion in London. Whether he be called' a High Commissioner, or by whatever other title he may be designated,

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
he should be regarded as the head of -that representative service which has to deal with the affairs of Canada abroad.
I do not know where my hon. friend got the idea, but he spoke about the possibility of appointing a minister to London. I want to assure him that so far as we on this side of the house are concerned, so far as the government is concerned, we have never thought of anything of the kind.
That was the word used in many press articles.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I agree that the press may have used the word, and I think my hon. friend was right in directing attention to the fact that "-minister" would not be an accurate designation of Canada's representative in London. It would -not be accurate, first of all, for the reasons which my hon. friend gave; and moreover it would be certain to be confused with "minister of the crown". The last thing I should wish to see, carrying out the doctrines of responsible government, would be a minister of the crown from Canada residing in London and there without opportunities of consultation with his colleagues, committing the administration of this country to whatever he might wish to say or do. There is another factor of importance, and that is the difference which must always obtain within the empire in the relation of one who represents merely a government and not the crown and one who represents not merely the government of his country but also the sovereign or recognized -head of the country from which he comes. May I make this a little clearer by way of illustration. Within the empire, the crown is represented in Great Britain by the King and in this Dominion by His Excellency the Governor General. The government of Great Britain, as distinct from the cr-own, has in Canada no representative at the present time. Such however is not the present position of the United States in Canada, which by its minister is represented both as respects the president and the government. Among other subjects discussed by Mr. Amery when passing through Ottawa was this very question of a representative to be appointed from Great Britain -to this dominion. The Secretary of State for the Dominions made it clear that it was -the intention of the British government to appoint a representative who would reside at Ottawa. What his designation will be, or who will be chosen, is a matter for the British government to decide. Mr. Amery naturally wished to have an opportunity of conferring with his colleagues in England before announcing any decision on either of these particulars, and he is returning with certain
views after having carefully considered the situation durin-g his visit to this country. Whoever is sent by Britain to represent the British government will receive a very cordial and warm welcome to this Dominion. I believe that the effect of personal representation of the British government at 'Ottawa will go very far to make closer and more effective the consultation which is so desirable if there is to be effective cooperation between the British government and our government; that it will make that consultation -much more effective than it has been hitherto. Having said this,
I now say to my hon. friend: If personal conference and contact is desirable as between governments of the British Empire, why is it not equally desirable with respect to the governments of the British Empire in their relations to the governments of other countries? The British government -has thought it advisable to -have a representative of His Majesty and- His Majesty's government in all parts of the world. That has proven to be in the interests of Great Britain. Why should it be less in the interests of His Majesty's government i-n Canada to have its representatives in other parts of the world? True, there is no necessity for having a number of representatives; we must gauge -the situation in each case as vve feel the necessity of so doing.
I submit, however, that in Europe conditions have vastly changed from what they were when Canada was first given representation there. It was in 1888 that Sir John A. Macdonald appointed a high commissioner or commissioner general to Paris. For forty years Canada has been represented in Paris by a commissioner general. In the intervening period there have been cataclysmic changes. In the recent past no less than four empires have disappeared, no less than twelve or thirteen new republics have come into being. The whole complexion of the map of Europe has altered. A league of nations has come into existence. This Dominion of Canada is a nation in the League of Nations, as it is a nation in the community of British nations. Not only is .Canada represented in the assembly of the League of Nations but it has a representative on the council of the league. I say therefore that conditions, so far as Europe is concerned, are entirely different from what they were at the time the commissioner general to Paris was appointed. I think it will be conceded by all who have been in Paris and have met Hon. Mr. Roy, the Commissioner General, that he has established there a position very different from the one which it was expected a commissioner general would hold, and that his position is

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
in reality much more nearly that of a minister. By that I mean, a minister has the right, as representing his government, of immediate approach to the ministers of the government to which he is accredited. He has the authority to speak in the name of his government. Mr. Roy has time and again been accorded that right as a matter of courtesy by the French government and by the British Ambassador in Paris. It has, however, been as a matter of courtesy that the right has been conceded. Now we have come to the time where we feel that if there is to be equality of status and co-operation between the different self-governing communities of the British Empire there should also be an increased measure of responsibility on the part of each with respect to its own affairs. We feel that Canada's interests, which have grown so largely in the course of the years, will be safeguarded more effectively, that the business interests of this country in relation to France and the government of Canada in her relations to the government of France will all be in a better position, if our representative in Paris is given a standing similar to that which a number of other countries, many of them much smaller than Canada, enjoy in France at the present time, and, I might add, the British government correspondingly relieved of a measure of embarrassment and expense. We have thought it advisable therefore to take this step.
Now I turn to the orient, and let me first point out the change which has taken place in the situation there. I believe it is true that our trade with the orient to-day is greater than was the trade of Canada with the United Kingdom at the time the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into office. When that event took place Canada's trade with the United Kingdom stood at a certain figure. That figure is exceeded to-day, so I am informed, by the total trade of Canada with the orient. Now volume of trade is indicative of a variety of increasingly important interests, and while I think it is wholly desirable, as my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) said, that we should have trade commissioners, and an increasing number, scattered in different parts of the world, no trade commissioner as such, it must be remembered, has any right to approach the ministers of the government of the country in which he holds office, nor does he speak with any authority on behalf of the government by whom he may be employed. He is not a representative of that government, he is the agent of a government department. I may say that our government has received from trade commissioners in different parts of the

world repeated appeals that their status should be improved, that they should be given something of a diplomatic status; that Canada was suffering because they had not the status which would enable them on behalf of the dominion, to have those relations with the governments of the countries in which they were stationed which they felt was desirable in the interest of Canada.
We have appointed one representative to the United States. We intend to appoint a minister to France, who will be the sole representative on the continent of Europe, and one to Tokyo who will be the sole representative on the continent of Asia. To appoint but one representative in Europe, one in Asia, in addition to one in America, each of whom will 'have the standing of ministers and be in a position to meet the diplomats and members of governments of other countries on an equal footing, is surely not in the present stage of our international relations proceeding with undue haste. And may I say to my hon. friend that the purpose we have in view in this matter is not at all that of emphasizing our status. That is not our view. We do not need to emphasize our status; our status is conceded and we are no longer worrying about it. But what we do maintain is this, that if there is to be equality of status there must be something also in the way of responsibility with respect to our own affairs, foreign as well as domestic, in whatever pertains to the relations between this dominion and other countries of the world. What we wish is to assume the responsibility which we as a nation, having to deal in increasing measure with foreign affairs, feel we should assume in the position to which Canada has attained at the present time. This I submit, is essential to effective cooperation with other parts of the empire.
May I say one further word in regard to our representation in the orient? Here I touch on a very large subject, and I hope the house will receive what I have to say as coming from a profound conviction of what I sincerely and deeply believe is of importance in the relations of this country with the orient. I was sorry to see at the party convention which my hon. friend attended that among other resolutions which were passed was a resolution declaring for oriental exclusion. I do not wish to question the motives of anyone in connection with the introduction or passing of that resolution.
I believe one can read it, as an hon. member from my hon. friend's own party has done, as not really meaning what it appears to say.

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
May I make this perfectly clear, that as regards desiring a white Canada and a white British Columbia, as regards desiring to maintain the standards of our labour in British Columbia, I will yield place to no one in the belief that we must not permit competition of the oriental races with our own people in that province? I think the numbers that have come into this country from the orient are excessive already and there is abundant reason why every possible measure compatible with good relations and good will between the different nations of the world should be adopted in order that we may prevent what I believe would be a very serious consequence were, for example, labourers from the orient to be permitted to come to this country in any numbers. But what I do say is this, that in dealing with foreign countries, a country with a population as large as that of Canada, a country as important as this country is, cannot afford to fail to take cognizance of the susceptibilities of the nations with which they are doing business and with which they wish to deal not only this year but for years to come. Hon. members know very well that there is no term more offensive to the Japanese people than the word "exclusion". I feel that in this parliament on these matters of foreign affairs my hon. friend opposite and myself ought to be able to unite in taking a question of this kind completely out of the realm of party politics. Let us agree that we do not want oriental labour coming into this country in competition with our own. But let us realize this, that if we are going to remain, as I hope and pray we always shall remain, a part of the British Empire, we owe a certain obligation to be true not only to ourselves but to other parts of the British Empire in our relations with and attitude towards other countries of the world.
During the time I was privileged to- be present at the meetings of the Imperial conference I learned a good deal about the difficulties which were confronting Great Britain in some of her foreign relations. Indeed, if not the main purpose of the conference, it always seemed. to me to be the most important result of the conference that those who came from other parts of the empire were afforded an opportunity of coming to appreciate the magnitude of some of the problems with which Great Britain herself had to deal and the importance of certain considerations with respect thereto. I believe that within the last year or two there has been no problem which Britain has had to face that in the seriousness of its aspect has been comparable with that of the unrest
which has developed in China, and which in the last session of this parliament led to discussions as to whether or not there was to be war in the orient and whether or not this country was to participate in it. Along with that unrest in China, stimulated as there is every reason to believe it has been from some other parts of the world, there has been great unrest in India. If to the unrest in India and the unrest in China you give the Japanese nation cause to feel indignation and resentment at the British Empire, I do not know what the consequences are going to be. I wish to say to my hon. friends opposite that when the government was face to face with the situation created by that resolution, and was forced to ask itself how, in the faoe of it, it was to deal with this oriental problem, then, and for the first time, we took the position that we could not stand for restriction of immigration by a policy of exclusion in those terms, but that we would do our utmost by diplomatic endeavour with a friendly nation to see that the numbers of Japanese coming into this country were reduced to the lowest possible point in a manner which at the same time would help to preserve the friendly relations between that country and ourselves and between that country and the British Empire.

Perhaps my right hon.
friend will explain what he said a moment ago that there were too many of them now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I meant exactly what I said. I would say so to-morrow in Japan. I think there are too many Japanese of the labouring classes in British Columbia at the present time. I have always made that clear. My hon. friend turned to the Speaker yesterday and complimented His Honour uipon his visit to Japan and the result of his diplomatic mission some twenty years ago. Does my hon. friend think we would have succeeded even at that time in getting the reduced numbers we succeeded in getting if the whole matter had been left to despatches or to the roundabout process of dealing through the Foreign Office in Great Britain with the Foreign Office in Japan? It was because we were able to send from Canada one of our own citizens, one of our own ministers, and have him deal at first hand with the Japanese government that at that particular time we w-ere able to make the arrangement we did. There was one remark which my hon. friend made yesterday that I did not like. I hope I was wrong in what I gathered as to the meaning of his reference to the diplomatic skill of this

The Address-Mr. Mackenzie King
country. I contend that the diplomatic skill of Canada with respect to Canadian affairs is of just as high an order as the diplomatic skill of Great Britain or that of any other part of the British Empire.
I made no reference to the diplomatic skill of Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am glad to hear my hon. friend say that.
Where a gentleman has been able to remain in power from 1921 to 1926, as my right hon. friend has, I have a high regard for his diplomatic skill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I can tell my hon. friend he will come to have a still higher regard if he just continues where he is for another half a dozen years.
It will not be that long.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: May I conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that it has been solely from a desire of meeting the responsibilities of Canada as one of the sister dominions of the British Empire, to play our part with respect to Canadian affairs as we believe we should play it in foreign relations as well as in domestic relations with a full consciousness of our responsibilities, that we have been led to take the step we have taken with regard to representation in Europe and in Asia and of which we hope this house will approve. In other words, our desire in these particulars as respects our country in its relation to other parts of the British Empire is expressed by the three words: equality, cooperation and responsibility. We believe in the' equality of the British nations within the empire; we wish to co-operate in a friendly and helpful way with all parts of the empire, and we wish in cooperating to assume to the full the responsibilities which as a nation within the British Empire we believe are ours in imperial and international affairs.

Mr. Speaker, before addressing myself to some of the important problems with which we in Canada are confronted, I should like to be permitted to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) who moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I can assure him that I enjoyed his address very much and I hope he will be long with us in this house to give us the benefit of his opinions. I had also the pleasure this morning of reading the translation of the speech of the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) who seconded the

address in reply to the speech from the throne. I enjoyed very much the reading of it, and I regret that I do not sufficiently understand the French language to have been able to follow him when he was speaking.
I wish also to thank the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) for his kindly reference to me yesterday. I am quite sure it was a mistake on his part during the proceedings on Thursday in this house when he forgot to make the reference, which forgetfulness he deplored. I accept his explanation and I appreciate his reference.
It will not be possible for me, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the forty minute rule is now in effect, to give to this house a detailed consideration of some of the more important questions with which I should like to deal, but so far as this group is concerned, no doubt different speakers will take up specific questions and give them a more detailed survey than it is possible for me to do in the time at my disposal this afternoon. I shall therefore lose no further time, and turn my attention to one or two of the more important matters.
The speech from the throne this year is not a document such as it was last year. It is not very specific. It is, in my judgment, merely a recital of circumstances or things which have already taken place. It gives to the House no intimation of the legislative program of the government for this session. In that respect the speech from the throne is very deficient. It is regrettable that the members of the house will have no intimation until such time as the actual legislation is brought down of what the legislative program which we shall have to consider later on will be. Comparing the speech from the throne this year with that of last year, a tremendous difference is to be noted. Last year the government did give the house a very good forecast of the legislation it intended to bring down, so that the members were apprised beforehand of what they might expect and were therefore in a position to study the different subjects that were coming up. But the speech this year is very deficient in that regard, and under no circumstances would we be justified in using extravagant language in praising it.
Since the house prorogued last year I have had the privilege of addressing many meetings of electors in my own constituency, and of telling those people that for once in the history of this country we had a government in power that carried out its promises at least on one occasion, and that was this government during the last session. We all remember the session

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
of 1926 when a certain program was before this house containing important pieces of legislation. For certain reasons which we all understand it was impossible to carry out that program at that time, but I had the pleasure of telling the people of my constituency that when the same government came into power again last year, they were in a position to carry out and did carry out their previous program, and we appreciate that very much indeed.
The speech from the throne states that we have evidences of great prosperity. It is quite true that we have exidences of greater prosperity than has prevailed for several years past. But is this prosperity general, or does it apply to certain sections of Canada and only to certain classes? I think we should find, if we were to review the situation very closely, that certain classes in Canada are probably fairly prosperous, but that on the other hand many other classes in Canada can by no stretch of the imagination be called prosperous. As a matter of fact if you go into our large cities to-day I think you will still find bread lines, notwithstanding all these evidences of prosperity that are spoken of, and because of that fact I feel that the speech from the throne is not as explicit in that respect as it should be. I think we all realize that certain sections of the country are not enjoying the same measure of prosperity as are other sections. There may be economic reasons why some sections of this country are not enjoying the same measure of prosperity as others are, but without going into those reasons there is no doubt at all that such sections do exist in Canada.
Dealing with the question of unemployment, which also is related to the question of prosperity, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in his address to the house yesterday afternoon cited the fact that we had imported during the last fiscal year $80,000 000 more of goods than we did the previous year, and he attempted to show to the house that if we had not imported this extra volume of goods we would probably have had no unemployment problem in Canada. I think my hon. friend is sufficient of a business man and has had a wide enough experience to know that all business is an exchange of goods and services, whether it be between individuals or nations; consequently if Canada is to export her surplus products-and in some lines of production we have a surplus in great abundance -it is necessary for us also to import. In that connection I should like to point out that there is some information which is
lacking at present and which would be of great value to the members of this house if it could be secured. We recognize, of course, that we are borrowing large sums of money from the different countries of the world for development purposes, railroad construction and the like, for loans for settlers and so forth, and that all our governments, federal, provincial and municipal, are borrowing large sums of money abroad. Now the only way in which we can pay back the principal and keep up the interest payments on these borrowings is by exporting our goods and selling them in the markets of the world. But we have no record at the present time of just what our annual obligations under this heading are, and I would suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that for the better information of the house and of the country generally, steps should be taken to secure that information as rapidly as possible so that we may have an intelligent idea of what our real balance of trade is at the present time. We do not know whether or not the balance of trade which is indicated as being in our favour is a real balance of trade, because we may owe in principal and interest more than the balance that is indicated in our favour. Under these circumstances, therefore, we are discussing this very important question more or less in the dark-merely stabbing at it instead of dealing with it in the light of full knowledge. I would again urge the Minister of Finance to take steps to make this information available to the house.
A great deal has been said, not only in this house but throughout the country, as to the necessity for securing capital to develop our natural resources and to build up industry. I should like to place this viewpoint before the house for its consideration. First of all, let us determine what capital is. Money is not capital. Money in its proper form is merely a medium of exchange, a medium whereby services or goods of one class are exchanged for services or goods of another. Money, therefore, being a medium of exchange, is not and can never be capital in the proper sense of the word. Real capital consists of lands for building purposes, the buildings erected upon these lands for manufacturing or productive purposes, the machinery of production and the raw material necessary for the product. That is the real capital. Whenever any person advocates the importation of large amounts of capital he must at the same time advocate the importation of large volumes of goods. Capital does not come into this country in the form of money. It comes first of all by way of credits.

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
After the credits are distributed, as they are intended to be distributed, there must follow the importation of goods either from the country of the origin of this credit or from some other country; consequently when we ask for the importation of capital or the increase of capital from outside sources we are asking for the importation of goods, and those who are of a protective frame of mind naturally would object to that. The two terms are not synonymous, and they can never agree in any shape or form.
The situation appears to me to be this: We have in this country undoubtedly a surplus of labour at the present time. Probably that surplus is not so great to-day as it has been in years gone by, but nevertheless we have a surplus of labour. We have the raw material from the natural resources to which that labour can be applied, and in most cases we have the necessary machinery of production. I wish to ask this question in all sincerity of all members of the house; is there any reason why we Canadians cannot create our own capital in our own way to suit our own needs? I maintain that it is quite possible for us, if we so desire and if we organize properly, to produce our own capital without importing it, and without at the same time having to pay interest for the use of it. This is a matter of very great importance. It is a big question, I admit, but no effort, so far as I am aware, has been made along those lines for the creation of our own capital. I am not at all satisfied that it is a good policy for the Canadian people to advocate the importation of large volumes of capital which eventually will have to be repaid and at the same time pay dividends upon it. I believe that, in the interests of the people of Canada, the working classes and all classes, it is very essential that we create the most of our own capital, to be used for our own services, in order that we may create a larger measure of happiness amongst all classes of Canadian people.
I should like to refer for a few moments to the conditions in western Canada. It has been said that we in western Canada have harvested the seaond largest crop in the history of the three prairie provinces. While that is true so far as the number of bushels is concerned, on the other hand we regret to say that the quality of that crop this year s in many respects very low, and consequently (he monetary return to the farmers of western Canada will not be as large as we had anticipated prior to the harvesting season.
It is only of value for export.

That is quite true.
Under those circumstances we do not expect to have the same measure of prosperity, measured by our purchasing power, as we had anticipated. We have had great losses from natural causes. During this year we have had more damage from hail in western Canada-at least in Saskatchewan and Alberta- than we have ever seen before. That has hit some sections and some farmers very hard, almost to the extent of putting them out of business. We also have had considerable damage from frost. That, of course, is a natural cause which you cannot overcome except by securing early ripening kinds of grain. Probably the greatest problem we have before us to-day is the question of rust. I want to pay a compliment to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) for his desire and his effort to try to secure ways and means to combat this menace to our welfare in the west. I should like also to point out to the government in this regard that, so far as the investigation of this particular matter is concerned, we require the services of the best trained minds that we can secure. It is so important a question that we cannot afford to be penny-wise in regard to it, and it is necessary to pay higher salaries than we are paying to-day in order to obtain .the services of the right class of men to assist us in this great problem. I would suggest to the government and to this house that it would be far better to pay those salaries in the hope of securing some remedy than that the western country should be subjected to the tremendous loss it now has to bear.
Hear, hear.

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
In the prairie provinces we are still confronted with railway problems. We appreciate the legislation that wTas passed by this house last session for 'branch line construction in connection with the Canadian National Railways. We appreciate also that the Canadian Pacific Railway is doing its duty to the best of its ability in providing branch lines. But there are still many districts unprovided with the necessary transportation, and until it is provided it will be impossible for them to produce to their utmost, and consequently Canada will suffer just to that extent. May we hope that another branch line program for the Canadian National Railway system will be in evidence this session, and that the Canadian Pacific Railway will also take similar action in regard to its system?
I now come to one of the important questions that has been discussed in this debate. I refer to the Hudson Bay railway. For years western Canada has felt that great injustice had been done to it because of the failure to complete this railway. Last year the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) intimated to the house that before any further expenditures would be made on a terminus an independent investigator would be sent into the territory to determine whether Port Nelson was feasible or whether another port should be selected. I wish to thank the minister for his kindness in sending me a copy of Mr. Palmer's report, which I have perused with a good deal of interest. From the data furnished by Mr. Palmer it is evident to me that a great mistake was made when Port-Nelson was selected as the terminus of the Hudson Bay railway. I also had the privilege of discussing this question with a friend of mine who was in that territory for three years with a survey party taking soundings at Fort Churchill and in the waters adjacent to Port Nelson. He informed me that in the judgment of those engaged in that survey Port-Nelson was not a very good place to provide shipping facilities, and that in fact Churchill was superior in every way. I trust, however, that no mistake will be made in selecting Fort Churchill as the terminus. I do not know just to what extent the government has committed this house and the country to expenditures at that point. I can quite understand their desire to ensure the completion of this work at the earliest possible moment; on the other hand, I think the government in matters of this description should be very careful not to take into their own hands that power which in the final analysis is vested in the House of Commons.

If my hon. friend will
permit, is he suggesting that that was done in this matter?

I am referring , now
more particularly to expenditures. I said I did not know just exactly how far the government had gone. If no expenditures of any great importance have been made, then I think probably the attitude of the government is quite correct; but outside of the question of the terminus to be selected, if those expenditures have been sufficiently large, then probably there is some reason for complaint.
I must remind my hon. friends that I am subject to a time limit.
I would request that the hon. -gentleman be given consideration for this interruption.

I am glad to accept the minister's explanation, and in the light of the evidence produced by Mr. Palmer I can congratulate him on the action he has taken in the matter.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

When the house rose at six o'clock I was about to deal with the question of immigration. I was very glad indeed to hear the statement of the Prime Minister this afternoon, to the effect that if the house deemed it desirable the whole question of immigration would be sent to one of the committees for -investigation. "I believe that would be the best way to deal with the situation, because we need to have an immigration policy suitable to the conditions which prevail to-day. We must remember that the conditions which obtained in 1900, and for some years thereafter, were altogether different from what they are to-day, and the new conditions demand the adoption of new immigration methods. From 1900 onward a large amount of railway construction was done in Canada,.

The Address-Mr. Gardiner
and an extensive area of crown lands was available for settlement. Under those conditions it was possible to absorb large numbers of immigrants annually. But to-day there is not the same amount of railway construction, which provides employment for new settlers, nor have we the same extent of crown lands from which to make grants to new settlers. In my judgment a land settlement policy is essential. Not only do we need such a policy but we must take care that no greater number of immigrants are to be admitted to Canada than the country is in a position at the time to absorb. I appreciate very much the suggestion the Prime Minister made in this regard. At present there is a partial land settlement scheme in operation in conjunction with the imperial government, but I understand that this will take care of only some three thousand families, and I should not be at all surprised to hear that the specified number of families have already been settled under that policy. We must review the whole situation and see if it is not possible to adopt a more effective policy with respect to immigrants than the one which is now being followed. I have had several interviews with men who claim to be in touch with the situation, and I have been informed by these men that many immigrants are coming from Great Britain under the assisted passage scheme, but instead of going on the land they are crowding into the cities. It is an easy matter for them to do so at points contiguous to large centres of population. The result is that under that particular policy we are getting immigrants who come to Canada at the reduced rate and then go to swell the population of our cities, which is certainly not in the best interests of Canada. I approve very heartily of a strict medical examination of immigrants, but complaints have come from different sources as to the severity of this examination in Great Britain. I have also received complaints with respect to the medical examination on the continent, but it is claimed that the examination there is not so severe as it is in the old country. If so, British immigrants to Canada are in a measure discriminated against. I do not know whether or not the statement is correct.

There have not
been any examinations made on the continent as yet, and very few have been made in the old country up to thfe present.

I accept the explanation. I am merely bringing these matters to the attention of the government so that they may take cognizance of them.
I wish now to deal for a few moments, if I may, with the case of the returned soldiers, whose situation is becoming more pressing each day. I should like to see this matter also referred to a committee for investigation. There are many veterans who require a medical examination but have not the needed funds to pay for medical attention; they are unable to follow any employment and consequently are almost destitute. It may be quite true that the Minister of Health has not at present the power to take care of this particular class of men, but some remedial legislation is necessary in their interests and that legislation is long overdue. These men have served their country faithfully and their health is now impaired. Whether that condition is or is not due to war service, in my opinion, makes no difference. I believe it is the duty of the country to see that these men who have served Canada so faithfully should be given such medical care as it is within the province of this parliament to grant. I appeal strongly to the house on behalf of this particular class of men, because I know many of them are in poor health and have not the means to secure that medical care which they should receive.
My time has pretty well elapsed, consequently I shall not be able to deal with many other matters which I desire to discuss. For instance, there is the question of grants to highways. We had in this country a policy by which there was a grant of $20,000,000, I believe, to assist the provinces in building highways. I maintain that the federal government has a duty to perform in regard to interprovincial highways and I trust that before the session is over this matter of assistance to the provinces to build particularly interprovincial highways will be given serious consideration by the house.
Then there is the question of technical education. We had a grant from this parliament for the assistance of technical education in the provinces. Some of the provinces have built suitable institutions for the purpose, but when the grant is withdrawn or has expired they will not be in a position financially to carry on this good work. Technical education is very important to all classes in Canada in that it makes our workmen and our people generally more efficient in their life work.
There is also the important question of the rate for Alberta coal. I will not attempt to-night to go into that, because time forbids, but I trust some of our members from Alberta will have an opportunity of dealing very extensively with that particular matter.
As regards the question of the St. Lawrence development, we are partial to that develop-
The Address

Mr. Gardiner

ment, yet we believe that much more information should be secured before that work is proceeded with. We are sympathetic in regard to the matter and that is about as far as we can go at present.
I have not the time to deal with the question of the tariff advisory board and its reports, except to remind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that at all times members of this house should be in a position to secure reports of the evidence given, before that board. If the question is one of funds, I trust that before parliament prorogues such funds will be made available.
I have not the time also to deal with the question of the redemption of the national debt and its being put on a sound financial basis. Up to the present we have merely taken the surpluses that accrue each year for the reduction of that debt, and in my judgment that is not good business procedure. Certain items should be included annually in the estimates until the national debt is much reduced.
I have just half a minute at my disposal and I am going to fake it in order to enter a protest here. We have listened with a good deal of interest to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and also the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in their addresses to this house. I was particularly interested in the Prime Minister's address this afternoon, more especially on constitutional questions. The Prime Minister spoke for something like three hours and twenty minutes, and while we all appreciate the value of his address, at the same time it seems somewhat incongruous in a democratic organization such as this. The last redistribution took place on a population basis; that is to say, each constituency had about the same number .of inhabitants in it, the quota being something like 36,000 souls. That means that each member of this house is responsible for the representation of a similar number of electors, but under the rule of last session a discrimination has crept in. At that particular time I did not appreciate the importance of the change in the rule limiting most of the members of this house to forty minute speeches, but if this rule is continued, an undemocratic situation will be created, and at this time I merely appeal to the house to re-consider that rule.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in most of what the
last speaker (Mr. Gardiner) has said I heartily concur. To-night, however, I should like to emphasize particularly certain matters in which the Labour group whom I represent

are interested. The speech from the throne as an indication of the government's program is distinctly disappointing; indeed it would almost seem as if the speech were becoming simply a convenient peg on which to hang a very elaborate ceremonial. I should like, however, to compliment the government on one or two matters which have been introduced, and I wish to refer first of all to the proposed appointment of a minister to Japan. It seems to me that action recognises not only the wider responsibilities which are facing us in Canada, but at the same time the importance of a situation which prevails on the Pacific coast. I refer also to the announcement that the government intend to give substantial assistance to industrial and scientific research. That it seems to me is a distinct step in advance.
The speech makes reference to the prosperity of the country. The hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Usley), in his very graceful speech, admitted that the prosperity was not as evenly distributed as it might have been, and he went on to say that he referred particularly to the territorial distribution. I would agree with him with regard to that matter. Certainly the central provinces are enjoying a larger measure of prosperity than either the east or the west, but I wish to refer particularly to the distribution as between classes. According to the latest statistics which are available in the Canada Year Book of 1926, the capital invested in manufactures amounts to 13,538,813,460, the net value of the products to $1,256,643,901, and the wages to 8420.269,496. The percentage of wages to the value added by the manufacture is 33.4 per cent. When the labourer receives only one-third of the added value which his labour produces, I do not much wonder that the other classes who receive the remaining two-thirds rejoice in the great prosperity. What does that one-third amount to in the case of the individual wage-earner? The average yearly wage is only $972, or roughly, $81 a month, or only $20 a week. I ask: How can a man live and maintain a decent standard of living on that amount, and how can the country generally be prosperous if the purchasing power of the mass of the workers is so low as that? I do not mean to say that this has anything to do with politics. It is ridiculous that either the leader of the government or the leader of the opposition should suggest that. This is but an indication of the great economic laws that are at work. Recently we have had from the census bureau of the United States Department of Commerce a report covering a survey which has been made of all the branches of manufacturing in the United
JANUARY 31, 192S	B9
The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
States. The report points out that industry is being centralized at an appalling pace; that the number of workers employed is decreasing, while the output and the manufacturers' profits are advancing with giant strides. Let me quote one 'brief paragraph from this report.
The outstanding features of the report were the increase in production, the decrease in employment of wage-earners and the increase in horse power.
If we want to know what low wages mean to the countryside I do not know that we can do very much better than take the statement that was made the other day by the member for Hull county in the provincial house at Quebec. He is reported to have said:
The labourers of Hull received only twenty-five cents an hour or $2.50 a day for a ten-hour day, and often lost working time during the year, and most of them had eight, ten or twelve children at home, and very often more. How could he keep them on $400 a year, which was all he had when he had paid his own board and contributed even lightly to the church and good works.
Yesterday when the Prime Minister was speaking about the growing employment in the country, he quoted the Premier of Ontario as refusing to acknowledge that there was unemployment in Ontario. May I say that in my judgment the Prime Minister was hardly fair because he has in his possession a letter recently received from Premier Bracken of my own province of Manitoba, in which that province points out the very serious state of unemployment, and asks the federal government to assist in giving relief. In a memorandum presented on December 14th by the committee on unemployment, of the provincial house of Manitoba, these statements are made:
In 1927, during the first seven days of December, 708 men registered for work at the employment office, as compared with 466 during the same period last year. There is also an increase in the number applying to the social welfare commission of Winnipeg for unemployment relief, the total number registered for relief to December 7, 1927, being 108 families as compared with less than half that number last year. Employment office officials estimate that there are 1,000 men available for immediate employment if work was available, and that this number is being added to daily through the fact that many men are coming to Winnipeg hoping to find employment in the Flin Flon development work.
Again:
The control of the immigration stream is in federal hands, and it would seem reasonable to demand that at least a share of the cost of relief made necessary by unemployment caused by immigration should be paid by the Dominion government.
We are told that there is a "substantial increase in the number of British immigrants." I should like to read quite a typical paragraph with regard to the British immigrant:
With neither employment nor money and only a few threadbare clothes to keep out the biting blasts and sub-zero temperatures, Stanley Hornsby, a young lad giving his address as "the old country", appeared in St. Boniface police court this morning charged with vagrancy, and pleaded with the magistrate to send him to jail.
That was on December 15th, the day after the provincial committee had reported on the question of unemployment, and it indicates how serious a matter unemployment is in the lives of our citizens.
On the other hand, the speech from the throne calls attention to the prosperity of certain classes. It mentions " increased railway receipts ", In that connection I note that a few months ago there appeared the following item in our daily papers:
The directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway to-day decided to issue an offer to shareholders of record August 19th, on the basis of one share to eight of their respective holdings, $32,500,000 of ordinary capital stock at $150 per share.
And I read the following comment from one of our labour papers:
The only explanation which will fit all the facts is that the Canadian Pacific Railway increases its capitalization by one-eighth to enable themselves to divide up the accumulated surplus profits and to prevent the surplus profits "piling" up in future years as an accusation of extortion and an argument for reduced transportation rates-and in the meantime the Dominion railway commission putters with little details such as railway crossings.
Lest that should be thought to be merely an extreme statement by a radical labour paper, perhaps I might quote from a letter that I received from a very good Liberal friend of mine, a Winnipeg lawyer, with regard to this very practice. He says:
There should be no cutting of melons in public utility corporations, and every such utility should be compelled to sell new stock on the open market for the best price that it will bring and the financiers of the utility therefore receive the full benefit of a sale of new stock.
I wonder why the government cannot put on the statute books legislation which will carry out the idea behind that quotation.
The speech tells us that there is to be the establishment of "more favourable trade relations between Canada and certain foreign countries." I hope the government will take the very earliest opportunity of informing the house why it broke off relations with Russia. There are no charges of improper activities on the part of the Soviet representatives in Canada. In a statement to the press the

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
Prime Minister explicitly repudiated any such thing. Let me. quote a comment from the Manchester Guardian on the action of the British government in severing relations with Russia:
Can British trade benefit? Quite the contrary. Will Europe in general be. the more tranquil for this widening of the chasm between Great Britain and Russia? Obviously not.
Again:
It is questionable whether we or Russia suffered more from the wars of intervention after the armistice. If we are now to attempt in the economic field what we could not achieve by force of arms, the consequences are likely to be equally costly to ourselves, to Russia, and to the peace of Europe.
Why, I ask, should the Liberal government in Canada be tied to the apron strings of the Conservative party of Great Britain?
I see the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) in his seat. I should like to offer him a suggestion with regard to the Hudson Bay railway and incidentally may I say that I think he is to be commended on his promptness in securing competent authority to make investigations with regard to the terminal of that railway. Amongst our most highly respected [DOT] immigrants in western. Canada are the Icelandic people, who came to this country over fifty years ago. Some of us perhaps fail to remember that their claim to be the real discoverers of America when Leif Ericson crossed the Atlantic is really fairly well substantiated. Two years from now the Icelandic people propose to celebrate the one-thousandth anniversary of parliamentary institutions along modern lines in Iceland. Large numbers of them are then returning to participate in those celebrations. I would like to suggest to the minister that, if. for nothing more than a matter of publicity, he should offer to send a party of these people to Iceland on one of the merchant marine vessels via Fort Churchill. As they say in the press, Ihat would certainly put Fort Churchill on the map.
We are informed that the government is "continuing negotiations with the prairie provinces for the return of their natural resources.'' I cannot say that that is exactly news. In fact, I am afraid if the negotiations go on for any great length of time longer there will be nothing left to return. Seriously, it seems to me that we are in danger of giving away our great natural resources of the north country, and I hope that at a convenient opportunity the government will tell the house just why it is that the Whitney syndicate is to be allowed to pay no royalties for a period of twenty years. I notice that
{Mr. Woodsworth.]
the Canadian Mining Reporter, speaking with regard to this matter, publishes the following:
The thing is wrong in principle. It is not because the Flin Flon deal is being made with foreign interests. It would stink just as badly if purely Canadian financial interests were being handed such a gift on a platter. What we object to is the giving away of our Canadian heritage by our government to anybody.
Here we really enter upon the wider question of the control of the natural resources. In that same northern district we have the White Mud falls. In my judgment the control of the powers of the White Mud falls is just about as important a question as that which was brought up last year in regard to the Georgian bay canal scheme. Why are these powers so recklessly alienated? I came across an article the other day in the Nation's Business for October, headed "Why our factories cross the border.'' The writer is Mr. Floyd S. Chambers, editor of the Financial Post, Toronto. He referred to the 1,400 American branch factories located in Canada and went on to speak of the United States having three billion one hundred thousand dollars invested in Canada, representing a mortgage of twelve per cent on the total national wealth of the country. If already twelve per cent of our national wealth is mortgaged to the United States, I submit it may not be so very long before we realize the evil consequences of the get-rich-quick policy that has characterized some of our business men of to-day.
At the last annual meeting of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, Mr. Cyril T. Young, in an address on Canada's Resources, exhibited a large map of Canada decorated with the union jack. He exclaimed dramatically "Long may the union jack flutter and wave," and of course there was applause. That sounds well, but I would call attention to the very rapid acquisition of our resources b>
Americans. Pulpwood, mining, oil, water-powers are passing under foreign control. Some day, if the house will permit it, I should like to exhibit in this chamber a spot map on which the American controlled industries would be marked with the stars and stripes. If that were done in respect to all of the country there would hardly be room to place the union jack, much less a Canadian flag, if we had one. Do not let us deceive ourselves by saying that because we live north of the forty-ninth parallel we control things here. Economic control and economic considerations are more important than political control or geographical considerations. Last summer I spent a month in a mining town in the mountains. When I was having supper

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
one evening in a miner's house a whistle blew. I think it was three blasts that signalled across the valley, and the miner remarked: "That means no work to-morrow." He had no option. And who was it who told him he should not work to-morrow? The company, of course-an American company with the stock owned in Pennsylvania and the board of directors sitting in the city of Philadelphia. My hon. friends around about me from Alberta are very anxious that we should adopt a policy of buying and consuming Canadian coal.
Hear, hear.

And I say to my
hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Garland) who says "hear, hear," let us examine the matter closely. When I do so I find it impossible to get up any great enthusiasm over buying coal mined in Alberta if the dividends go into the pockets of the men who are controlling the mines in Pennsylvania.
Hear, hear.
Hear, hear.

That is a matter
that will have to be considered in the days to come. The leader of the opposition warns us against "selling our estate." I agree with him, but I would ask him, can we look to him to deliver us from the control of those big corporations so very largely American in character? Before the election, I was interested in reading some of the guesses that were being made as to the Conservative leadership. In MacLean's Magazine, August 15th, there was an article headed, "Who's the Tory Moses?" The article says:
Still it seems a pretty safe bet that Cahan will be proposed by powers which operate usually in St. James street, Montreal. A leader from Quebec must be suggested, if only to make impressive the apparent transfer of support to some other man.
