Since there has
been so little legislation forecast in the speech I should like to suggest some measures that it seems to us ought to have been included. Perhaps the house hardly recognizes very clearly what are Canada's obligations under the labour section of the Peace treaty and the Washington conventions. I hold in my hand a very interesting memorandum issued by the Labour department showing the extent to which our obligations are met by existing legislation. This is rather a naive document. I should like to give a few illustrative extracts. Reference is made to the eight-hour day and forty-eight-hour week, with this comment:
Legislative jurisdiction is primarily vested in the provinces.
And so with a number of other provisions. Reference is made to persons engaged in work for the Dominion government. Here we have Canada's own admitted responsibility. The memorandum merely says:
The convention is partly met.
There is a clause with regard to mutual arrangements among members who have established systems of unemployment insurance. The memorandum says:

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
This has no application to Canada, as no system of insurance against unemployment has been established jn this country.	_
A very easy way of getting out of it. Then there is a clause with regard to the prohibition of -night work for women. This is delightful:
The provincial statutes vary in the length of the night period during which this class of employment is forbidden.
What class of unemployment is that?

Night work for
women. Again, reference is made to weekly rest in industrial undertakings. At last we have reached what is clearly federal jurisdiction. This is admitted, "as it involves jurisdiction relating to the criminal law." But what does the memorandum say?
It is met by the provisions of the Lord's Day Act.
Well, Mr. Speaker, in the language of the street, I would say, "it is to laugh"! Can we forget that there are large groups of labour in this country still working twelve hours a day and while there is a rest day once a fortnight it is earned by continuous work for twenty-four hours? Yet we are told that these clauses, part of a solemn treaty, are being met by the Lord's Day Act-yes, I was almost making another slip and saying, the Lord's Day Alliance Act.
Then there is a clause for the prohibition of the use of white lead in painting. This the memorandum says is:
Within provincial jurisdiction. . . no laws.
I would ask, why should not this come under the criminal code? If white lead poisoning is inimical to human welfare, even to human life, why should not its use in painting be made a crime in this country, as I understand it has been elsewhere? Again, there is a clause dealing with workmen's compensation and equality of treatment for national and foreign workers. Just listen to what the memorandum says in relation to this:
The practice varies in different provinces. . . in Ontario and Manitoba residents of countries which were enemies in the Great war are not entitled to compensation.
And this, notwithstanding the fact that we entered into the most solemn obligations with enemy countries.

Who says
all this? We missed the origin of this.

I thought I made
it clear that these clauses are included in the Peace treaty of Versailles, and that I am

quoting from a memorandum issued by the Department of Labour of the federal government, showing how far we have legislation covering these points in the treaty.
There is provision in the Versailles treaty for compulsory sickness insurance. The memorandum of our Department of Labour says frankly:
There is no legislation on this subject in Canada.
In that connection may I say that my colleague from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) is asking the house this session at least to go so far as to appoint a committee to consider this matter and see what can be done in the premises. As to unemployment insurance for seamen, the memorandum simply has to say:
No legislation.
Then, "prevention of unemployment in agriculture." Why, I would have thought this had something to do with the protection of harvesters. Is that the case? Not at all, for all the memorandum tells us on this head is that we have:
Provincial and private land settlement.
What a joke! Mr. Bryce M. Stewart in a recent book dealing with these Canadian labour laws and the treaty says:
In the matter of actual ratification Canada stands in the lower ranks despite her rating as one of the foremost agricultural and the sixth industrial country in the League of Nations. While certain provinces have recognized some of the conventions in legislation, and indeed have surpassed them in some instances, no single province has taken action on all the proposals, nor have all the provinces recognized any one.
Of course, division of powers between the Dominion and the provinces is pleaded as an excuse but, sir, let me give you a quotation which occurs in an entirely different connection. The Royal Securities Corporation condemns the inaction of the United States federal government with regard to the diversion of water at Chicago, which it characterizes as:
A flagrant violation of principles recognized by the law of nations and founded on abstract justice.
I would suggest that the following judgment pronounced on the United States with regard to water diversion applies with equal force to Canada in this matter of the ratification of the labour clauses of the treaty of Versailles:
The prolonged incapacity of the United States federal government to deal with this-
Water diversion.
-is a significant measure of its weakness and a warning to those who would rely upon its treaty undertakings if they happen to conflict with the interests of individual states.

Have we no sense of honour in Canada that we could enter into these most solemn obligations, which apparently there has been practically no effort -made to have implemented?
Will my hon. friend allow me? Does he take into account the declaration that was made by one of the signatories to the treaty, that one hour before they signed it they had never seen it?

Would it
have made any difference?
I do not know whether it would have made any difference or not.
Well, it might have as far as the moral engagement is concerned.

I think the hon. member for Labelle will agree that we have certain responsibilities, and that if a nation undertakes to sign a treaty there is surely some obligation on its part to see that that treaty is lived up to.
But is it not true that non-repudiation during the many years which have since elapsed would fully meet the question of the hon. member for La-belle?

Possibly. I was very glad to see that the Conservative convention at Winnipeg pledged itself to carrying out the treaty. I cannot see where the difficulty lies. The Prime Minister has written a book on Industry and Humanity. He is in favour of carrying out these obligations, the Conservatives are in f-avour; then why cannot we have the treaty carried out in its entirety?
I should like to have had time to call attention to other classes of social legislation which are long overdue. For example, the Old Age Pensions Act which was passed in this house last session gave pensions to certain classes of people of seventy years and over. I would point out that the railway companies are dismissing men at the age of sixty-five. It seems to me that if men are being turned off at that age, provision ought to be made for taking care of them before they reach the age of seventy.
And may I point out that a resolution of this house was passed some years ago by which prisoners in our penitentiaries were to be paid for their work, and in the case of married men the money was to be turned over to their families. So far as I have been able to learn, the Department of Justice has not proceeded to act on that resolution; in fact we have the rather anomalous situation
of the superintendent of penitentiaries begging that some action be taken along this line. He is reported:
To keep men in enforced idleness is not only most inhuman, but in one institution in a foreign country where it has been tried over thirteen per cent of the unfortunate inmates were driven insane in one year.
In regard to the Dominion of Canada he says:
Only one-tentli of the work possible to be done is being done. The government spends many thousands of dollars yearly for furniture, furnishing and equipment of various kinds, a portion of which could easily be made in the penitentiaries.
It does seem to me that when we have gone to the trouble for two years in succession of debating this question on the floor of the house, and have definitely passed a resolution, the matter ought not to be disregarded in this way.

My hon. friend must
remember that many of the labour organizations have unfortunately, for many years past, adopted resolutions petitioning the government against any sort of labour being carried on in penitentiaries. We have that situation to meet.

Yes, but I would
point out that the object has been merely to ensure that prison labour shall not come into competition with free labour. I may say that labour is quite content to have our prisoners do many types of work that could be done in prison, work which is needed in this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, like other hon. members I have been keeping my eye on my watch and I see that the time allotted to me is nearly up. I should have liked to discuss the larger questions in which we are becoming more and more related to international affairs, but unfortunately I cannot do so in the time at my disposal. I content myself at this juncture with directing the attention of the house to a resolution which is being placed on the order paper by my colleague from East Calgary (Mr. Adshead), to the effect that:
-the government of Canada should discuss with the government of Great Britain the desirability of Canada accepting article 36 of the statutes of the Permanent Court of International Justice providing for compulsory arbitration in international disputes.
With the feeling that is developing in some parts of the United States against Great Britain and the feeling which is developing in some parts of Great Britain against the United States-a feeling which is being voiced perhaps by rather irresponsible individuals, but which is nevertheless a reality that must

be reckoned with-I do not think that the present situation should be allowed to go unchecked. I fancy that some statement on the part of Canada looking to a better understanding in world affairs and a frank acceptance of the principle of arbitration would go a long way towards safeguarding the international situation.

I rise to make a few observations in what is a more or less formal debate in this house, particularly so when nothing in the nature of an amendment to the address has been moved. One has only ito read the address which His Excellency the Governor General delivered to parliament to realize that it is more in the nature of political propaganda than of a serious parliamentary document. The theory of the speech from the throne is that His Excellency shall give to parliament the reason or reasons for its being convened, and it is quite proper in that speech to mention anything of national or international concern which has taken place since prorogation. 1 submit however that in the present instance the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who is himself responsible for every word which is in that speech, has gone beyond all reason in his attempt to pat himself and his government upon the back in almost every clause of that document. We on this side of the house have no objection to his proclaiming in proper terms the prosperity which the country undoubtedly enjoys at the present time. But the object of the Prime Minister in so doing is to claim credit for himself and his government, while we on this side of the house are inclined to give the credit for the present happy condition to the vigour, to the intelligence and to the adaptability of' the people of Canada. Clause after clause of the speeoh from the throne is merely a chronicle of last year's events, something which the members of the house all know, something which does not need to be repeated and which is entirely out of place in a state document of this kind. I do not wonder that one of the leading newspapers of this city has seen fit to call attention editorially to this remarkable document.
Now there are one or two suggestions in the speech from the throne to the effect that we are to have some legislation. We are advised that two of the departments of the government are to be amalgamated. It is proper to place that in the speech; that is contemplated legislation. It is suggested that some measure will be introduced in regard to scientific research: that too is properly placed in the speech. And I believe that one

other measure is contemplated in regard to new trade agreements. But the rest of the speech consists in an attempt to display before the country the activities or inactivities of the ministers who preside over the various departments of. this government. It is solemnly stated in the speech from the throne that the government is considering the question of returning their natural resources to the three prairie provinces-something the government has been considering since 1922 or 1923. It is solemnly stated also that ministers are considering the question of returning railway belt lands to the province of British Columbia- something they have been considering for two or three years past. Who cares what amount of consideration they give these matters? What we ask for and what we expect is action in respect of them. There is no intimation of any action, and I suppose we may take it for granted that these ministers will simply continue their consideration of these important and pressing questions; and next year when this parliament is convened I for one should not be surprised if these matters were then still under consideration by the government.
However, we must take the program as it is. The debate on the address has wandered rather widely from the text of the address itself, and I intend only to dwell upon one or two matters which have been raised in the discussion. One of these matters, to my mind a most important matter, is the question of the Dominion finances. That question was raised purposely by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) with the object of drawing definitely to the attention of the government and of the Minister of Finance the absolute necessity of taking at once, at this session of the house, some definite action towards the retirement ultimately of the public debt of this country. This matter was raised in the house last session in a very able and well considered speech by my hon. friend from Toronto East Centre (Mr. Matthews). We raise it again now at the opening of the session and, in so far as an opposition is able to insist and demand, we propose to insist and we propose to demand that the government formulate some definite scheme whereby the debt of the Dominion of Canada may be retired within a reasonable number of years.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has in his possession all necessary data in regard to that question. Financial authorities throughout Canada have discussed it, and have reported upon it. It is not a very

The Address-Mr. Guthrie
difficult matter to deal with, and if the Finance minister will display some courage in the matter he can evolve a scheme whereby the debt of Canada can be paid within forty or fifty years at most without causing any inconvenience or any disruption of a serious kind to the finances of Canada. The province of Ontario has adopted a scheme. Five or six years ago when the present government took office in that province it was confronted with a very serious financial situation. Something had to be done. Experts were called in. Proposals were made; a plan was evolved, and to-day we find that that government is annually setting apart a sufficient sum of money to retire the whole indebtedness of the province, I think within thirty years, and so far no inconvenience has been found in carrying out that scheme. I submit that a similar course should be adopted in this house. We draw the matter as forcibly as we can to the attention of the government, and so far as an opposition has any power to do so, we demand and we insist that some action be taken at the present session towards the retirement of the public debt,.
One has only to examine the public accounts and financial statements made by the Prime Minister and from time to time by the Minister of Finance to conclude that the situation in regard to the debt of this country is not dealt with as satisfactorily as it should be. We hear statements from time to time on the platform and in this house that tremendous amounts have been paid off on this, that, or the other occasion. Newspapers give great prominence to statements of that kind, and we are all inclined to rejoice when we hear that the public debt has actually been reduced by large amounts. But when one sits down to examine the public accounts one is not as well satisfied with the results. Is it known in Canada that the actual funded debt of the country, the amount of money which we have to pay to creditors, for which we have given the bonds of this country signed, sealed and delivered by the Finance minister, is twenty odd millions higher to-day than it was when the King government took power? I make the statement from the Canada Gazette of December 31 last, and the statement is correct. The funded debt of Canada, for which creditors hold our bonds, was on the first day of this year $2,442,228,000, twenty-two millions more than it was when this government assumed office. The Prime Minister yesterday, in discussing the finances of Canada, announced amidst the applause of his supporters that in 1925-26 we had redeemed the bonds of Canada in cash to the
extent of $20,000,000; in 1926-27, $43,000,000; in 1927-28, $29,000,000, $8,000,000 and $18,000,000, making a total retirement of $118,000,000 in the funded debt of the dominion, and at the same time on the 31st December last we find that we have twenty odd millions more funded debt than we had when this government came into power.
Now here is the situation: In 1921, when this government came into office, the system followed in the Finance department in respect to the national railways was that when we met with a loss we went to the treasury and paid it, and we charged it to the national debt. For the two years following the defeat of the Meighen government in 1921, Mr. Fielding, the then Finance minister, did precisely the same thing; when he had a railway payment to make and deficits to meet he went to the treasury, paid them in cash, and charged them to the debt of Canada. But when Mr. Fielding passed out and another gentleman became Finance minister a new scheme was evolved, and I do not say a bad scheme. It was decided that thereafter all outlays and deficits in respect to the national railways should be charged to the railways and not to the national debt of Canada, and instead of coming forward in 1923, 1924 and 1925 with deficits, as there had been in years previously, the government were able to come forward with surpluses, as the public accounts show, because they charged up railway defaults not to the national debt but to special railway account. How did they raise the money for the railroads, you ask? In former days it was raised on the bonds of Canada and charged to the debt of Canada. But under the new regime they raised railroad money on the bonds of the railway companies, and instead of signing the face of the bonds the Finance minister endorsed the back of them, guaranteed their payment, and allowed them to be charged against the Canadian National railways. That is the way he works out his annual surplus. What about the sixty-five millions of bonds that were issued by the railways last year and guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada, far more than they retired? In former times, and under Mr. Fielding's administration in the Finance department, those bonds would have been charged to the national debt, but under the new system of bookkeeping they are charged to the Canadian National railways. The country is the guarantor and the country will ultimately have to pay the bonds.
Now passing to another aspect of the matter. These claims of reduction in the national debt puzzle me. They always have puzzled me,
The Address-Mr. Guthrie

but I have been more puzzled in t'he last two years since I have studied the budget speeches of the present Minister of Finance. The trouble is that his budget speeches do not jibe with the public accounts. Which shall we accept? I am accepting to-night the public accounts of Canada, and I turn to the 31st of March, 1922-I am pretty generous; I am going back three months after this government came into power-the net public debt of Canada was $2,422,000,000. On the 31st of December last I find that according to the Canada Gazette the net debt of Canada amounted to $2,281,000,000, or an apparent reduction of $141,000,000 in five years. But that is not the whole story. That is not a correct statement. It may be correct on its face, but on examination it will not stand. In the first place, in 1922 we had an issue out of $241,000,000 of Dominion notes, which are the medium of exchange whereby trade in this country is carried on; they constitute debt so long as they are outstanding. On the 31st of December last Dominion notes outstanding stood at only $193,000,000; Dominion notes to the amount of $48,000,000 had been called in and destroyed. When they call them in I think the term they use is that they "cremate" them; they burn them and get rid of their debt in that way. There were $48,000,000 more of Dominion notes current in 1922, and that $48,000,000 should be taken off the debt reduction, leaving, as I understand the matter, the net reduction at $93,000,000 instead of $141,000,000, and that after nearly six years' operation by the government in power to-day, and the whole amount of $93 000.000 of reduction is dlte to the improvement in Canadian National Railways returns.
I must take issue with the Prime Minister >n another point. In his speech of yester-lay and to-day he made a bold claim in regard to the question of reduction of taxation. I cannot agree with him in the statements he has made, and I am trying to make my statement from the public accounts of Canada laid before parliament by this government. I state that the taxes collected from the Canadian people during the past five years are far greater than those collected during the previous five years by their predecessors. What counts in the matter of taxation? It is the burden upon the people; that is the only test. When I hear the Prime Minister, or the Minister of Finance as he certainly spoke in the campaign in North Huron, making claims that certain taxes have been reduced I must express my amazement. Why is this government not candid enough to say:	The
taxes we have taken off are the taxes we have fMr. Guthrie.]
put on? They maintain that they have taken off the stamp tax on cheques. That tax was only two cents a cheque when they took office and they promptly increased it to two dollars a cheque as a maximum. Last year they cut it down to two cents on cheques for over ten dollars. The increase was made by the present government, and tardily and after much persuasion from this side of the house they saw fit last session to take off the increase and put the tax where it was when they took power.
They made claim on the platform at Goderich that they had taken off the stamp tax on receipts. Who put it on? It should never have been put on in the first place. It was put on against the protest of those who sit in the opposition in this chamber. Last year, after much persuasion from the opposition, they reluctantly removed it and they claim that as an achievement.
Do hon. members recollect the statement made in this house yesterday by the Prime Minister in regard to the sales tax? Why, he said, they had reduced it twenty per cent. Twenty per cent sounds pretty well, but what are the facts? When the present government came into power there was a war measure sales tax in this country imposed to meet the awful expense of the war, a temporary measure. What did it amount to? It amounted to one and one-half per cent on the manufacturer, one and one-half per cent on the jobber, or three per cent all told. That was the tax when this government took power in 1921, but they were hardly in office before they started raising taxes. During the first session they raised the sales tax to five per cent instead of three per cent and the following session they raised it to six per cent. Then they found it was so high that it actually interfered with the trade and commerce of the country and they cut it down to five per cent. With a great sound of trumpets and much applause last session a reluctant minister of finance said: "I will take one per cent off," and one per cent off five per cent is the twenty per cent reduction to which the Prime Minister referred yesterday. The sales tax with this one per cent reduction now stands at four per cent, but when this government came into power the tax stood at three per cent; and yet they have the audacity in this house and on the platform to claim a reduction in taxation in connection with the sales tax. Why did they not, take the advice of the opposition last year? We endeavoured to plead with them to remove this sales tax altogether, and today and during this session, if it is in the power of an oppositi'-'" to insist or demand

The Address-Mr. Guthrie
we are going to insist and demand that the sales tax be removed altogether. We went so far last year as to divide the house on, the question; we moved in the house that at least the sales tax be taken off wearing apparel and boots and shoes. Do you think, sir, the government would do that? No; every hon. member on the government side voted down that motion and every hon. member on the opposition side supported it. The sales tax stands at four per cent to-day-and what was the excuse of the Minister of Finance? "Oh," he said, "if you abolish it, it will practically ruin the retail merchants in this country."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear.

If the Minister of Finance had a little more courage on this and on other subjects it would be better for the Dominion of Canada and the trade of Canada. What my hon. friend lacks is courage. He is content to sit at his ease and allow the Department of Finance practically to run itself. A little 'courage is necessary in that important department, and if he will take the courageous course and in his budget will wipe out that iniquitous sales tax he will have not only the support of the members of this house but the approval, of ninety per cent of the people of the Dominion of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I did that I would have to come back, or another government later would have to come back, and pay the automobile people as we paid them for remissions made by Sir Thomas White.

I am afraid my hon.
friend sees lions in the path. Let him have courage and he can do this. What about the burden of taxation in this country? This claim of reduction of taxes is so absurd, so unfounded, that it must be exposed.
I take the taxes collected from the people of Canada for the last five years. I take the customs tariff tax. I know that it is not admitted on all hands that that is a tax, but for the purpose of my statement I am going to include that as one of the taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend claim that it is a tax?

I did not express any
opinion. I say I am including it in this calculation, and I am including also the sales tax, the stamp tax, the income tax, and all the other burdens which this government has imposed on the people of Canada. I take all those taxes imposed over a period of five years. I cannot bring my figures up to December 31st last; I have to take the return laid before the house on March 31st last, and what do I find? For the five years from 1922 up to the 31st of March, 1927, the average amount of taxation taken annually from the people by this government was 3387,780,000. I take the five preceding years. I add together the same taxes, and I find that during that period the annual average amount of taxation collected was $348,500,000, or $39,280,000 less per annum than the average amount taken by the present government from the people of this country during the last five years.
Now how does that work out in the way of a burden upon the shoulders of the people of Canada? We can only take an estimate of the population, and the best one I can get is the one which was given to this house last session by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm)-evidently a carefully worked out figure; he estimated our population on the first of March last to be 9,390,000. On the basis of that estimate I find that the burden of taxation under this government is $4.18 per capita, or for a family of five, $20.90, more than it was during the five years preceding the advent to power of the present government. In the face of those figures, which are taken from the blue books prepared by this government, is it fair for the government to claim that there has been reduction of taxation? I have given you the taxation which the average individual in this country pays; I have given you the taxation which the average family of five in this country pays; I have taken the government's own figures, and their own estimate of population-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But my hon. friend has conveniently forgotten the debt which he himself ran up as a minister of the government from 1915 to 1921.

I discussed the debt question before I entered upon this phase. I realize that the debt in those years did increase, and increase enormously. I realize that the afterwar debt was as serious almost as the debt which had to be piled on year by year during the war, and I am glad to say that during those war years and after the war we had an administration and a minister of finance who did not Jack in courage.
I have given the house these figures taken from the government's own blue books. They can be checked up; if I am wrong I want to be put right, but I am satisfied that I am not wrong in the statement I have given. In the face of those figures, let me ask hon. members
The Address-Mr. Guthrie

opposite to be careful when they make platform statements about reductions of taxation by the present government. I think a little care should be exercised by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Finance when they discuss either in this house or on the public platforms the question of debt retirement, when we know full well from the public accounts that the actual bonded debt which we owe to creditors is greater to-day by S20.000.000 odd than it was when this government took office.
Let me advert to one other matter which has been discussed to-day, although it. does not arise very directly out of the speech from the throne. It is a question which was the subject of a good deal of discussion in this country and in this house about a year ago arising out of the report of the Imperial conference of 1926. The discussion which has taken place in this chamber during the last day or two as to whether we had or did not have equality of status with the motherland and the other dominions recalls very vividly the debates which took place in this chamber last session. I do not know that the matter has been very much advanced in the interval. I am inclined to be well satisfied with the statement of the Prime Minister of Great Britain made in these buildings last August, when he stated in the presence of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister that so far as Canada was concerned, no limitation had been imposed upon the powers which she enjoyed, and nothing new had been added. That. was a very satisfactory statement, as well as a very brief one, and carried out my own understanding of that document which we call the report of the Imperial conference of 1926. But the point which my hon. friend and leader sought to emphasize was merely this:	The Prime Minister
and his ministers are inclined at all times to state that that equality of status, to which I think we all look forward with a good deal of satisfaction, exists at the present time. As my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) said to-day, that it is an ideal not yet attained; I believe that is a correct statement of the situation, and until a committee of experts shall report upon some method or plan whereby certain imperial acts may be either repealed or abrogated or otherwise rendered non-effective, equality of status cannot be attained. I am not dissatisfied with the present situation in any respect; I am perfectly satisfied with it, but in my own view there is

another question, and a very important one, which can never be resolved in favour of equality of status. I doubt if actual equality as between the motherland and the dominions can ever be achieved. Where the force is, where the might is, where the power is, there is going to be the actual source, the real head of the state.

Would you call that
"functioning"?

It may be a "function",
as my hon. friend suggests. I had that thought in mind when my right hon. friend read that particular clause in the report today. The question in my mind is this: On that great question of war and peace can. we ever have equality of status? Shall we ever be in a position by any act of ours to declare war or to make peace on our own account? Can we by any act of ours involve the motherland, the other dominions and the empire in a war? No, we cannot. Can the mother country? Certainly. A declaration of war by the motherland involves this and every other dominion instanter, and it may be entirely against our will and against our desire. We may desire to avoid it, to dissociate ourselves from it entirely. That will not help us. Our land will be liable to attack, our commerce liable to be seized or destroyed, and our citizens to be taken as prisoners of war without any act of ours. Under circumstances of that kind can you have actual equality? I do not know that anybody ever desired such a thing. I for one do not. I am * absolutely satisfied with the position we have attained to-day, and I do not believe that in our generation, or in the generation to follow us, Canada can ever reach that plane of absolute equality, which is proclaimed in newspapers and political platforms, a position which we do not enjoy and which I do not believe we ever shall enjoy.

Does my hon. friend
express the view that Canada will always be in such a position that we shall have no voice in regard to war?

I did not say that. I said our declaration would not be upon the same basis as the declaration by Great Britain.
Much has been said and suggested in regard to the right, which we do not now enjoy, of amending our own constitution. I confess that I have no very strong opinion upon that matter. I think it might be well if that power were v'ven to this country. It is a

power or a privilege which is now enjoyed by practically all the other self-governing dominions. I do not mean that I would agree that the power to amend our constitution should be given to this parliament alone. I would not agree to that, but the power to amend our constitution should be given to this parliament and to the nine provincial legislatures. However, as the matter stands we suffer from no disadvantages in that respect. I am absolutely satisfied in my own mind, and my opinion has been confirmed by conversations with such men as Mr. Baldwin and others, that at any time when this parliament and the legislatures of the provinces can agree and ask for an amendment to our constitutional act, the British parliament will not hesitate to amend it. First we must agree on what we want, and the moment we do agree and properly present our request to the parliament of Great Britain, it will be granted; so that we suffer to-day from no disadvantage in that respect. Our difficulty is to agree among ourselves. We hope for much from the conference which was held between the Dominion government and the various provincial governments last autumn. We hope there may be some important results from that conference, but I am afraid that they merely agreed to disagree on the main questions which they were called upon to consider. Certainly, so far as I read the report, no agreement was reached upon the question of senate reform, and no agreement seems to have been reached in regard to the question of amendments to the constitution. I have no doubt that interchange of ideas among prominent men is always a matter of advantage, but I do not think that conference got much beyond an exchange of ideas. Nothing concrete seems to have resulted from it-nothing at all events of an important nature. But I maintain, and have always maintained, that we are suffering from no difficulty and no disadvantage whatever by reason of the fact that we have not in this country power to amend our own constitution. I think I would like to see Canada have the power through this parliament and the legislatures of the various provinces. Whether it would be an advantage or not I cannot say, but I believe it is accepted and constitutionally settled in Great Britain that whatever the parliament of Canada, with the consent of the legislatures of the Dominion, should ask in regard to our constitutional act would be engrafted upon the statute.
That is the principle that governs now.

That is the principle that governs now, and that is the principle that will always obtain. So that I do not feel very much concern myself about it, although the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) seems pretty strongly wedded to the idea that we should have the right to amend our own constitution. But I know at the same time that many of his compatriots in the province of Quebec, including the Premier of Quebec, take a directly opposite view to that of the Minister of Justice in that respect. They are quite content to abide by the British North America Act as it stands to-day, and that is my own view; I feel quite content to abide by it in the same way.
I do not desire to transgress the new rules, and therefore I resume my seat.

The statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon, in his very excellent address, that the government was prepared to return these natural resources to the prairie provinces and at the same time continue the subsidy at the present amount in lieu of lands which have been alienated, I think is most encouraging to say the least. Before resuming my seat I want to say a word on the tariff. The work of the tariff board has reached a point where the government should be in possession of sufficient facts to warrant some reductions in the tariff. I have followed the work of the board as closely as possible without having the verbatim reports of the hearings, and I would suggest to the government that reductions might well be made on some lines of clothing and on kitchen utensils without seriously affecting the manufacturers. Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to discuss the different items in the speech from the throne, for I consider that speech as more a recital of past events than a forecast of the legislation the government intend to introduce at the present session. In passing, however, I should like to refer to the prosperity which it is claimed Canada is enjoying at the present time, and to express my pleasure that that prosperity prevails to a greater extent than during the past few years. This I attribute mainly to the following five factors: the growth of the industry of agriculture, the increased production of forest products, the increase in our mineral production, the increase in the amount of capital that has recently been invested in the development of hydro-electric energy, and the increase in cur tourist traffic.
I think everyone will admit that during the past four or five years the yield of agricultural products has been above the average, and the price that has been obtained, particularly for the wheat from western Canada, has been such as to add very materially to the wealth of this country.
As to the increase in our forest products, which in value are second only to those of agriculture, their value for 1927 is said to be no less than $475,000,000, of which approximately $283,000,000 were exported, chiefly to the United States-a material factor in maintaining the trade balance at as favourable a figure as it is. Looming large in connection with forest products is the pulp and paper industry, which is the most important manufacturing industry in Canada to-day, keeping in mind not only the value of the finished product but also the wage and salary distribution. The Prime Minister (Mr. [DOT]JANUARY 31, 1928

Mackenzie King) said in his speech to-day that Canada had risen to first place in the world in the manufacture of newsprint. That statement is absolutely true. Canada, also occupies the proud position of exporting more newsprint than all the other nations of the world combined. In order to illustrate the growth of this industry let us compare the value of the product in 1913 with that of 1926. In the former year the total production of newsprint amounted to 350.000 short tons. In 1926 it had risen to 1,189,000 short tons, valued at $121,182,987, an increase in the newsprint production in that period of 438 per cent. The total production of pulp and paper for the fiscal year 1926 was $215,488,315.
Canada's rise to first place in the pulp and paper industry is due, in my opinion, to the wisdom and foresight of the provincial legislatures of Ontario and Quebec in placing an embargo on the export of pulpwood, notwithstanding what my hon* friend (Mr. Bancroft) has just said with respect to that action. I agree with my hon. friend, however, to this extent: I should like to see every stick of pulpwood that is cut manufactured in Canada, at least to the newsprint stage. If there is any discrimination against the actual settlers in Canada to-day surely some means can be devised whereby the settler shall be given a reasonable price for his wood, and yet maintain the manufacture in this country.
That is all he is asking.

Well, I think he should get it. When we consider the value of our forest products, the increased payroll which has come into existence as a result of the increase in the manufacture of those products during the last few years, and the increased capital which has been invested, not only in the enlargement of mills already in existence but in the erection of new mills, every one must admit that this development has played an important part in the prosperity that we are enjoying to-day. Then, as a result of the increase in the manufacture of newsprint, in the pulp and paper industry, and in mineral production, there has been a great demand for an increase in hydro-electric power, and as a result large sums of money have been expended in the development of hydro-electric energy. Let me give you a few figures to illustrate the growth of that development. The capital invested in hydroelectric development in 1910 was $121,000,000. To-day the capital invested is estimated at $900,000,000. an increase in seventeen years of over six hundred per cent. During the past three years over $180,000,000 of new

During the past few years we have benefited by another increasing source of revenue;
I refer to the tourist trade. A few years ago this was not regarded seriously but last year, according to the figures compiled at Washington and by our own government, over $200,000,000 was spent in Canada by tourists from the United States, and when we consider the amount expended here by tourists from other countries we should probably be well within the mark in estimating that almost a quarter of a billion of dollars was spent by tourists in Canada last year-surely no small factor in promoting the prosperity which Canada is enjoying to-day.

When we realize that between fifty-five and sixty per cent of the total area of Canada is contained within the pre-Cambrian shield or mineralized belt, we may form some idea of what we may expect in the future from the mineral development of this country.

There is a provision in the customs tariff to the effect that when structural steel is made in Canada in all sections weighing up to 120 pounds per yard the present duty applied to sections weighing less than 36 pounds per yard shall be applied to the larger sections. At the time this section was drafted practically none of the larger sections were made in Canada, and consequently had to be imported from foreign countries. Since then conditions have altered considerably. Canadian mills are now in a position to supply every need of the consumer in all the sections of steel angles and in beams up to six inches and channels up to seven inches. The Algoma Steel Corporation at Sault Ste. Marie has had the foundations laid for several years past for the erection of a mill to take care of the larger sections. For financial and other reasons they have not been able to complete that mill, but I am given to understand that they have informed the tariff commission and the government that if the clause of the tariff with respect to the larger sections of steel is made effective, they will immediately proceed to complete their mill at a capital expenditure of approximately $10,000,000, and will then be in a position to meet the Canadian demand for practically all the larger sections of steel.
